docs.title: KCP CLI
docs.text:
KCP is a CLI tool for planning and executing migrations to Confluent Cloud.

Note

KCP supports migrations from two source types:

  • AWS MSK (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka) — full discovery via AWS APIs + Kafka Admin API.
  • Apache Kafka (including Confluent Platform and other Kafka-API-compatible distributions) — direct scanning via Kafka Admin API.

The workflow differs slightly based on your source type. See the Command Reference for per-command specifics, or the Source Compatibility matrix for which commands support which source flavor (MSK Provisioned/Express, MSK Serverless, Apache Kafka).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Tip

Recommended: on macOS or Linux, install the latest stable release with the install script. It detects your OS/architecture, downloads the matching binary, verifies its checksum, and places it on your PATH:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/confluentinc/kcp/main/install.sh | sh

Pin a version with KCP_VERSION=v0.8.5 or change the target directory with KCP_INSTALL_DIR="$HOME/.local/bin".

Binaries are published for macOS, Linux (amd64/arm64), and Windows (amd64) with every release on GitHub. Each release includes these assets: kcp_darwin_amd64, kcp_darwin_arm64, kcp_linux_amd64, kcp_linux_arm64, and kcp_windows_amd64.exe.

Important

Always install a released binary. Building from the main branch produces an unreleased, in-development build — see CONTRIBUTING if you intend to build from source.

Run uname -m if you're unsure of your architecture: arm64 / aarch64 → arm64 build, x86_64 → amd64 build. Apple Silicon Macs are arm64; older Intel Macs are amd64.

To download manually instead of using the install script, the tabs below show the equivalent terminal flow for headless or scripted installs.

macOSLinuxWindows 
# Apple Silicon: PLATFORM=darwin_arm64. Intel: PLATFORM=darwin_amd64.
PLATFORM=darwin_arm64
LATEST_TAG=$(curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/confluentinc/kcp/releases/latest \
  | grep '"tag_name":' | sed -E 's/.*"([^"]+)".*/\1/')

curl -L -o kcp "https://github.com/confluentinc/kcp/releases/download/${LATEST_TAG}/kcp_${PLATFORM}"
chmod +x kcp
./kcp version

# Optional: put kcp on your PATH so you can run it from any directory
sudo mv kcp /usr/local/bin/kcp
kcp version

# PLATFORM=linux_amd64 or linux_arm64.
PLATFORM=linux_amd64
LATEST_TAG=$(curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/confluentinc/kcp/releases/latest \
  | grep '"tag_name":' | sed -E 's/.*"([^"]+)".*/\1/')

curl -L -o kcp "https://github.com/confluentinc/kcp/releases/download/${LATEST_TAG}/kcp_${PLATFORM}"
chmod +x kcp
./kcp version

# Optional: put kcp on your PATH so you can run it from any directory
sudo mv kcp /usr/local/bin/kcp
kcp version

Download kcp_windows_amd64.exe from the releases page, move it onto a folder on your PATH, and verify with kcp version.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
KCP uses the standard AWS credential chain for any command that calls AWS APIs. Supported auth methods:

  • Environment variables: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, and (optionally) AWS_SESSION_TOKEN.
  • AWS credentials file: configure with aws configure.
  • AWS SSO / Identity Center: aws sso login.
  • IAM roles: assumed roles or EC2 instance profiles.
  • Credential helpers: any tool that writes to the standard AWS credential locations (e.g. granted).

Verify with:

aws sts get-caller-identity

Each command's per-command AWS IAM permission requirements are documented on its page in the Command Reference.

Note

Apache Kafka migrations do not require AWS authentication. Apache Kafka clusters are accessed directly via Kafka Admin API using the credentials you provide in apache-kafka-credentials.yaml. See kcp scan clusters for details.

docs.title: High-Level Workflow
docs.text:
The typical migration flow:

  1. Discover / scan — kcp discover (MSK) or kcp scan clusters (MSK or Apache Kafka) to build kcp-state.json. See Getting started for the step-by-step runbook.
  2. Report — kcp report costs and kcp report metrics for cost and utilization analysis. Alternatively, use the kcp ui for fine-grained analysis.

  3. Generate migration assets for data migration:

  4. kcp iac <asset> generate for Terraform using target-infra, migration-infra, topics, schemas; kcp iac acls kafka|iam generate; kcp iac connectors msk|self-managed|connector-utility generate.

  5. kcp migration resources for direct creation on the destination cluster through the REST API for cluster links, topics and ACLs.

  6. Execute client switchover — kcp migration cutover execute (validates and runs the cutover in one command, continuing from the live state if an earlier run was interrupted; --dry-run validates only).

docs.title: Key infrastructure decisions
docs.text:
Before starting, decide on:

  1. Is your source Kafka cluster reachable over the public internet, or only from within a private VPC?
  2. If private, do you already have a bastion / jump host, or do you need one?
  3. What authentication methods are enabled on the source, and which will you use for the migration cluster link?

Only certain migration topologies are possible for a given combination — see kcp iac migration-infra generate for the type matrix.

docs.title: Bastion host requirements
docs.text:
• Public endpoints — you can run kcp commands directly from your local machine.
  • Private endpoints — kcp must run from inside the source VPC. Either:
  • Provision a new bastion with kcp iac bastion-host generate, or
  • Use an existing jump server and copy the kcp binary onto it.

Note

For private MSK, transfer the kcp binary to a host inside the same VPC before continuing.

docs.title: Command reference
docs.text:
The full CLI reference is generated directly from the Cobra command definitions and lives under Command Reference. Entry points:

  • kcp discover — scan AWS for MSK clusters
  • kcp scan — scan a Kafka cluster, S3 broker logs, or a schema registry
  • kcp report — generate cost and metrics reports
  • kcp iac — generate Terraform for target, migration, topic, schema, ACL and connector assets
  • kcp migration — cut clients over to Confluent Cloud through the Gateway (cutover) and create Kafka resources directly (resources)
  • kcp ui — launch the local web UI
  • kcp update / kcp version / kcp docs — housekeeping

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
This page is a runbook for the first thing you do with kcp: scan your Kafka clusters and look at the result. It takes you from an installed kcp to your clusters, topics, ACLs, consumer groups, connectors and schemas in kcp ui. For what comes after, see Next steps.

Discovery (MSK) and kcp scan clusters are the required steps. The other scans in step 3 are optional: run the ones that apply to your estate and skip the rest.

Every step has an MSK tab and an Apache Kafka tab; follow the one that matches your source. Confluent Platform clusters are scanned as Apache Kafka.

Everything is written to a single state file, kcp-state.json, which later commands read and extend. Every command is safe to re-run: new results are merged into the state file, not duplicated.

Step MSK Apache Kafka / Confluent Platform 1. Discover kcp discover not applicable 2. Set up credentials edit the generated msk-credentials.yaml write apache-kafka-credentials.yaml 3. Scan 3.1 Clusters kcp scan clusters kcp scan clusters (optionally with metrics) 3.2 Client activity (optional) kcp scan client-inventory not applicable 3.3 Schema registry (optional) kcp scan schema-registry kcp scan schema-registry 3.4 Connectors (optional) kcp scan msk-connectors, kcp scan self-managed-connectors kcp scan self-managed-connectors 4. Review kcp ui kcp ui

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
MSKApache Kafka

kcp needs AWS credentials for discovery and for the AWS-side scans; see Authentication. Your machine must also be able to reach the brokers, because kcp scan clusters connects with the Kafka Admin API. To see which IAM permissions each command needs, see its page in the command reference.

Your machine must be able to reach the brokers (and, for the optional scans, the Schema Registry and Kafka Connect REST endpoints). No AWS credentials are needed.

To run kcp from a container instead of installing the binary, see Running kcp in Docker, which shows how to run these same commands in a container.

Where a command needs a password, this page writes it as an environment variable ($sr_password, $connect_password). Export the variable first, or substitute the value directly in the command; either works.

docs.title: 1. Discover (MSK only)
docs.text:
MSKApache Kafka

kcp discover finds your MSK clusters and records their configuration, costs and CloudWatch metrics.

kcp discover --region us-east-1 --metrics-granularity 5m
  • --region takes one or more regions (repeat the flag or comma-separate them). To discover specific clusters instead, pass --cluster-arn.
  • --metrics-granularity sets the CloudWatch resolution: 60s, 5m, 1h or 1d (default 1d). Finer granularity gives more detail on bursty workloads but grows the state file; see kcp discover for the maximum time range of each.

This writes two files:

  • kcp-state.json: the clusters found and their discovered configuration.
  • msk-credentials.yaml: one entry per cluster, which you complete in the next step.

There is no discovery step for Apache Kafka. Go straight to step 2.

docs.title: 2. Set up credentials
docs.text:
MSKApache Kafka

Open the generated msk-credentials.yaml. For each cluster, kcp discover lists the authentication methods that cluster supports and enables one of them. The file looks like this (illustrative):

regions:
  - name: us-east-1
    clusters:
      - name: orders-prod
        arn: arn:aws:kafka:us-east-1:123456789012:cluster/orders-prod/abc-123
        auth_method:
          iam:
            use: false
          sasl_scram:
            use: true
            username: ""
            password: ""

How kcp scan clusters reads this file:

  • Each cluster with exactly one method enabled (use: true) is scanned. Enable a method on several clusters and all of them are scanned in the same run.
  • A cluster with no method enabled is skipped, with a warning. To scan only some of your clusters, leave the others disabled.
  • A cluster with more than one method enabled is an error. Pick one per cluster.
  • Fill in the details the method needs. A cluster that only supports SASL/SCRAM is written with that block enabled but an empty username and password.

Re-running kcp discover keeps the credentials you have already filled in for clusters it finds again.

Create apache-kafka-credentials.yaml describing how kcp connects to each cluster. This example is a cluster using SASL/PLAIN with a Prometheus server for historical metrics:

clusters:
  - id: prod-kafka
    bootstrap_servers:
      - broker1.example.com:9092
      - broker2.example.com:9092
    auth_method:
      sasl_plain:
        use: true
        username: client
        password: <password>
    prometheus:
      url: http://prometheus.example.com:9090
    metadata:
      environment: production
      location: us-east-1
  • id is the name kcp uses for the cluster in the state file. You pass the same value as --cluster-id in later steps.
  • Every entry under clusters is scanned, so list as many clusters as you like in one file.
  • auth_method takes exactly one block: sasl_scram, sasl_plain, tls, unauthenticated_tls or unauthenticated_plaintext.
  • prometheus (or jolokia) is only needed if you want metrics in step 3.1.

Every field, the TLS options and more worked examples are in Apache Kafka credentials.

docs.title: 3. Scan
docs.text: kcp scan has one subcommand per kind of resource, and each adds its results to the same state file. Start with clusters; the rest are optional.

docs.title: 3.1 Clusters
docs.text:
kcp scan clusters connects to each cluster with the Kafka Admin API and records its topics, ACLs and consumer groups in kcp-state.json.

MSKApache Kafka 
kcp scan clusters --source-type msk \
    --state-file kcp-state.json \
    --credentials-file msk-credentials.yaml

A cluster that could not be scanned is reported with a warning and skipped; the rest are still scanned.

Topics, ACLs and consumer groups only:

kcp scan clusters --source-type apache-kafka \
    --state-file kcp-state.json \
    --credentials-file apache-kafka-credentials.yaml

To also collect broker metrics, add one of the following. Both need the matching block in the credentials file, and both feed the same reports.

Historical metrics from Prometheus (needs a prometheus block):

kcp scan clusters --source-type apache-kafka \
    --state-file kcp-state.json \
    --credentials-file apache-kafka-credentials.yaml \
    --metrics prometheus --metrics-range 7d

Live metrics polled from each broker's Jolokia endpoint (needs a jolokia block):

kcp scan clusters --source-type apache-kafka \
    --state-file kcp-state.json \
    --credentials-file apache-kafka-credentials.yaml \
    --metrics jolokia --metrics-duration 5m --metrics-interval 10s

See Metrics collection for the metrics recorded and how rates are calculated.

Use --skip-topics, --skip-acls or --skip-consumer-groups to leave any of those out. Reading a consumer group's type needs brokers on Kafka 3.8 or newer; see the command reference for what is recorded for each group type.

docs.title: 3.2 Optional: client activity (MSK only)
docs.text:
MSKApache Kafka

kcp scan client-inventory reads the broker logs in S3 to work out which clients (producers and consumers) are using each cluster. This tells you what has to move at switchover.

It needs, on the source cluster:

  • Trace logging on every broker: kafka.server.KafkaApis=TRACE.
  • Broker logs delivered to S3.

Point --s3-uri at the folder of logs for the period you want to analyse (logs are delivered into one folder per hour):

kcp scan client-inventory \
    --state-file kcp-state.json \
    --s3-uri s3://<bucket>/AWSLogs/<account-id>/KafkaBrokerLogs/<region>/<cluster-name>-<cluster-id>/<yyyy-mm-dd-hh>/

Each client is recorded once, keyed by client ID, topic, role, authentication and principal, so you can run this again on another time window and only new clients are added.

Not available for Apache Kafka: the scan reads MSK broker logs from S3.

docs.title: 3.3 Optional: schema registry
docs.text:
kcp scan schema-registry records every schema and version in the registry. --sr-type confluent works with any registry that exposes a Confluent-compatible REST API, including Apicurio through its /apis/ccompat/v7 endpoint.

Confluent Schema Registry with basic authentication:

kcp scan schema-registry --sr-type confluent \
    --state-file kcp-state.json \
    --url https://schema-registry.example.com:8081 \
    --use-basic-auth --username sr-admin --password "$sr_password"

Use --use-unauthenticated instead of the basic-auth flags for an open registry, or --use-mtls with --tls-client-cert and --tls-client-key for mutual TLS. If the registry is HTTPS behind a private CA, add --tls-ca-cert.

AWS Glue Schema Registry (uses your AWS credentials):

kcp scan schema-registry --sr-type glue \
    --state-file kcp-state.json \
    --region us-east-1 --registry-name my-glue-registry

Run it once per registry.

docs.title: 3.4 Optional: connectors
docs.text:
MSKApache Kafka

MSK Connect connectors are matched to the MSK clusters already in your state file:

kcp scan msk-connectors --state-file kcp-state.json --region us-east-1

To limit the scan to one cluster, use --cluster-arn instead of --region. Add --metrics-granularity (60s, 5m, 1h or 1d) to also collect the connectors' CloudWatch metrics.

Self-managed Kafka Connect workers are scanned through their REST API. --cluster-id is the ARN of the MSK cluster the connectors belong to:

kcp scan self-managed-connectors \
    --state-file kcp-state.json \
    --connect-rest-url http://connect.example.com:8083 \
    --cluster-id arn:aws:kafka:us-east-1:123456789012:cluster/orders-prod/abc-123 \
    --use-basic-auth --username connect-admin --password "$connect_password"

Kafka Connect workers are scanned through their REST API. --cluster-id is the id of the cluster in your credentials file:

kcp scan self-managed-connectors \
    --state-file kcp-state.json \
    --connect-rest-url http://connect.example.com:8083 \
    --cluster-id prod-kafka \
    --source-type osk \
    --use-basic-auth --username connect-admin --password "$connect_password"

For an open Connect REST API use --use-unauthenticated; for mutual TLS use --use-tls with --tls-client-cert and --tls-client-key. Sensitive connector configuration values are redacted before they are written to the state file. To also collect Connect worker metrics, see Connect metrics collection.

docs.title: 4. Review the result
docs.text:
Open the state file in the UI:

kcp ui --state-file kcp-state.json

The UI runs locally on http://localhost:5556; see kcp ui. Open each cluster and check that what you expect is there: its topics, ACLs and consumer groups, plus the metrics, clients, schemas and connectors from any optional scans you ran. If something is missing, re-run the relevant scan with --verbose to see the detail.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• kcp report: cost and metrics reports from the state file.
  • kcp iac: generate Terraform for the target, migration infrastructure, topics, schemas, ACLs and connectors.
  • Getting Started with Zero-Cut Migrations: initialize and execute the client switchover.

docs.title: Migration Plan
docs.text: Source: Amazon MSK · Generated · kcp 0.0.0-localdev · scanned 2026-09-04 12:00 UTC

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1 cluster across 1 region. Each cluster gets one migration plan, split into an infrastructure half and an application half. Where a cluster runs multiple apps with different needs, the application half is per app.

Migration plan Region Infrastructure plan Application plan clickstream us-east-1 Ready Ready

No throughput metrics were scanned, so all sizing below is a lower bound. Run kcp discover --region <your-region> (without --skip-metrics) to size from real ingress/egress before you commit.

0 required + 5 optional questions open across all plans.

Prefer a hand? Talk to a person. A Confluent migration specialist can walk through this plan with you, for free.

docs.title: Cluster: clickstream (us-east-1)
docs.text: Source: MSK Provisioned · 180 topics · 6 brokers · auth: AWS IAM, SASL/SCRAM

docs.title: Infrastructure plan
docs.text:
Ready

Category Recommendation Why Cluster type Enterprise Private networking is a hard requirement you set, and that starts at Enterprise. docs Sizing Autoscales, nothing to provision We size from your partition count (the only signal we have); measured ingress/egress can raise this. docs Networking PNI + Egress PrivateLink Endpoint PNI (Private Network Interface) scales to the full 32 eCKU (elastic Confluent Unit for Kafka), so it grows with you. The Egress PrivateLink Endpoint is added so the migration cluster link can reach your source cluster, which PNI doesn't carry. docs Authentication API keys (SASL/PLAIN) Default baseline you can change with target_auth; Confluent Cloud issues new credentials after cutover. docs

Sized from your scan: 1,500 partitions. Not measured: ingress throughput, egress throughput, request rate.

docs.title: Why these recommendations
docs.text:
• Cluster type: Based on your answer (private networking required), an Enterprise cluster fits: private networking starts at Enterprise, and nothing else you told us pushes it up to Dedicated. Zones: Spread across 3 Availability Zones, with a published uptime SLA up to 99.99% for this cluster type once you provision 2 or more eCKU (elastic Confluent Unit for Kafka). See the cluster-type docs for the SLA terms.
  • Sizing: Based on your scan (1,500 partitions), we size from your partition count (the only signal we have); measured ingress/egress can raise this. This tier scales with your workload, so there is no capacity for you to pick.
  • Heads up: Sizing is a lower bound; see the note at the top of the plan.
  • Networking: Based on your answer (private networking required), on AWS, we recommend PNI (Private Network Interface) for your private connection. It scales to the full 32 eCKU (elastic Confluent Unit for Kafka), so it grows with you. Confluent Cloud pulls your data over the cluster link, reaching out to your source cluster. PNI doesn't carry Cluster Linking traffic, so the link needs an Egress PrivateLink Endpoint alongside PNI.
  • Authentication: After cutover, your clients authenticate to Confluent Cloud with API keys (SASL/PLAIN). This is the default baseline; OAuth and mTLS are also available if you need them. Your applications' API keys belong to Confluent Cloud service accounts. Your Kafka ACLs don't carry over with your data. Recreate them in Confluent Cloud: kcp create-asset migrate-acls kafka turns the ACLs from your kcp scan into Terraform, with a Confluent Cloud service account and its ACLs for each principal. Review the generated files before you apply them. Your AWS IAM policies don't carry over with your data. kcp create-asset migrate-acls iam reads the IAM policies of the roles and users you name and turns their Kafka actions into Confluent Cloud ACLs, as Terraform. It reads only the first resource in each policy statement and ignores conditions, so check each generated ACL against the policy it came from.

docs.title: Application plan
docs.text:
Ready

Category Recommendation Why Data migration Cluster Linking, all at once (Restart-All-At-Once) We recommend a Cluster Linking cutover, moving all your clients over together in one scheduled window. docs Schema Schema Linking Your registry can reach Confluent Cloud, so we recommend Schema Linking. docs Connectors None to move There is no connector work in this plan. Topics Topics should mirror as they are Your topics carry over as they are. docs Historical data No separate backfill to plan There's nothing to re-fetch from object storage. docs

docs.title: Why these recommendations
docs.text:
• Data migration: Based on your answer (a scheduled window, all at once), we recommend a Cluster Linking cutover, moving all your clients over together in one scheduled window. Before you cut over, enable consumer offset sync on the cluster link: set consumer.offset.sync.enable=true and list the consumer groups to migrate in consumer.offset.group.filters (it defaults to none), so consumer offsets come across too. At cutover, stop your producers and consumers, wait for the mirror to catch up (lag zero) and one consumer offset sync interval, promote the mirror topics so they accept writes, then restart your clients against Confluent Cloud.
  • Schema: Based on your answer (Confluent Platform Enterprise 7.1+, migrate your schemas), your registry can reach Confluent Cloud, so we recommend Schema Linking. It preserves your schema IDs, and no client change is needed for the schema move.
  • Connectors: Based on your answer (no MSK Connect or self-managed Connect), there is no connector work in this plan.
  • Topics: Based on your answer (topic settings match the defaults), your topics carry over as they are.
  • Historical data: Based on your scan (no tiered storage), there's nothing to re-fetch from object storage. Your data migration still copies everything your topics currently retain, so if they keep a lot of data, plan a cutover window long enough to move it. Run kcp discover --region <your-region> (without --skip-metrics) to size the retained data.

docs.title: Migration steps
docs.text:
Before you start. The steps below read these from your state file. Run any scan you haven't already, so the state file has them:

  • Schemas: kcp scan schema-registry --state-file demo-scan.json --sr-type confluent --url <source-sr-url> --use-unauthenticated (or --use-basic-auth / --use-mtls with its credentials)

Build the infrastructure this plan recommends, then move your data over it. kcp generates the Terraform for each step; you review it and terraform apply.

Step 1: create the target cluster. Create an Enterprise cluster with PNI + Egress PrivateLink Endpoint networking in the Confluent Cloud Console, or Talk to a person to set it up with a specialist. kcp create-asset target-infra isn't used here: it builds PrivateLink networking, not PNI, so it can't provision the networking this plan recommends. Set up PNI + Egress PrivateLink Endpoint networking on it and API keys (SASL/PLAIN) client authentication, and note its environment ID, cluster ID, bootstrap endpoint, and REST endpoint for the later steps. The migration link's Egress PrivateLink Endpoint is added in the link step below.

If you would rather use PrivateLink than PNI, kcp create-asset target-infra (docs) builds the environment, the cluster, and PrivateLink networking:

kcp create-asset target-infra \
  --state-file demo-scan.json \
  --source-cluster-id arn:aws:kafka:us-east-1:123456789012:cluster/clickstream/b2 \
  --needs-environment --env-name <your-env-name> \
  --needs-cluster --cluster-name <your-cluster-name> --cluster-type enterprise \
  --needs-private-link --subnet-cidrs <your-subnet-cidrs>

Step 2: prepare your source credentials. What the link needs to sign in to your source, by method:

  • AWS IAM: Nothing to do for IAM here. The cluster link uses your existing SASL/SCRAM path (above), so your MSK cluster is unchanged for the migration; your IAM clients get new Confluent Cloud credentials when you point them over. Your plan's authentication recommendation covers how to recreate your AWS IAM permissions in Confluent Cloud.
  • SASL/SCRAM: No change. Cluster Linking uses your SCRAM credentials as-is. The link's user needs READ and DESCRIBE_CONFIGS on the topics you mirror, and DESCRIBE on the consumer groups.

Step 3: build the migration link. Your data migration runs over the recommended link (Private source with external outbound cluster link (SASL/SCRAM), --type 2). Your source is private and its brokers use SASL/SCRAM, so the cluster link reaches it privately, over an external outbound endpoint, using your source's SASL/SCRAM credentials. Fill in the placeholders (the cluster you created plus a link name), then terraform apply:

kcp create-asset migration-infra \
  --type 2 \
  --source-type msk \
  --state-file demo-scan.json \
  --cluster-id arn:aws:kafka:us-east-1:123456789012:cluster/clickstream/b2 \
  --cc-type commercial \
  --target-cluster-type enterprise \
  --cluster-link-name <your-link-name> \
  --target-cluster-id <cc-cluster-id> \
  --target-rest-endpoint <cc-rest-endpoint> \
  --target-environment-id <cc-env-id>
  • <your-link-name>: a name you choose for the cluster link, for example msk-to-cc.
  • <cc-env-id>, <cc-cluster-id>, <cc-rest-endpoint>: from the cluster you created.

Alternative: a jump cluster in your VPC (SASL/SCRAM), if Confluent Cloud can't reach your brokers over an egress endpoint. That is --type 4, which needs extra jump-cluster inputs (a bootstrap endpoint, an existing PrivateLink endpoint, and subnet CIDRs). See the docs.

Step 4: create your topics on the target. Recreate your source topics as mirror topics that the cluster link forwards your data into, with their partition counts and configs, using kcp create-asset migrate-topics (docs):

kcp create-asset migrate-topics \
  --mode mirror \
  --source-type msk \
  --state-file demo-scan.json \
  --cluster-id arn:aws:kafka:us-east-1:123456789012:cluster/clickstream/b2 \
  --cc-type commercial \
  --target-cluster-id <cc-cluster-id> \
  --target-rest-endpoint <cc-rest-endpoint> \
  --cluster-link-name <your-link-name>

Step 5: migrate your schemas. Copy the source schemas into Confluent Cloud Schema Registry; the Schema recommendation above covers the approach. Run kcp create-asset migrate-schemas (docs):

kcp create-asset migrate-schemas \
  --url <source-sr-url> \
  --state-file demo-scan.json \
  --cc-type commercial \
  --cc-sr-rest-endpoint <cc-sr-rest-endpoint>

Step 6: run the cutover. Before you cut over, enable consumer offset sync on the cluster link: set consumer.offset.sync.enable=true and list the consumer groups to migrate in consumer.offset.group.filters (it defaults to none), so consumer offsets come across too. In the properties file, set consumer.offset.sync.enable=true and consumer.offset.group.filters={"groupFilters":[{"name":"<consumer-group>","patternType":"LITERAL","filterType":"INCLUDE"}]}. Then run confluent kafka link configuration update <your-link-name> --config <your-link-config-file> (docs). At cutover, stop your producers and consumers, wait for the mirror to catch up (lag zero) and one consumer offset sync interval, promote the mirror topics so they accept writes, then restart your clients against Confluent Cloud.

What changes for each client app at cutover: point it at the new Confluent Cloud bootstrap endpoint; switch its security config to API keys (SASL/PLAIN) with the new Confluent Cloud credentials; and, for any app that uses Schema Registry, point it at the new Confluent Cloud Schema Registry URL.

At cutover, stop the schema exporter and set the Confluent Cloud Schema Registry back to READWRITE, so producers can register new schemas.

Backing out: until you promote the mirror topics, nothing is committed: your source keeps taking writes until you stop your producers and cut over. To roll back, restart your producers against the still-running source instead of promoting the mirror.

Step 7: decommission. Delete the cluster link and the Egress PrivateLink Endpoint, then retire your source cluster.

Access control (set up separately). Your source's authorization rules don't carry over. Recreate them with kcp create-asset migrate-acls iam and kcp create-asset migrate-acls kafka. The Authentication recommendation above covers what it reads. Do this before cutover. This is independent of moving your data — plan it alongside the steps above, not after.
