docs.title: Run a Migration Cutover
docs.text: To carry out a cutover through Confluent Gateway, run kcp migration cutover execute with your migration manifest. This page explains how execute and lag-check use the manifest, how kcp resumes an interrupted migration or conversion, and what to check before you run a cutover.

docs.title: Execution model
docs.text:
The migration manifest drives a resumable migration workflow:

  • execute validates the manifest and live infrastructure. It reads the live initial Gateway custom resource (CR) to check that the route's mode matches the declared migration type (see Declare the migration type) and, on a static route, to derive the bootstrap server ID from the target domain. It then carries the migration forward through fence → promote → switch (a conversion: fence → verify → sync offsets → switch). Every run reconciles live from the manifest and the current cluster state, so you can safely continue an interrupted run by re-running the same command: it resumes from whatever the live world already reflects. It re-reads the manifest (topology and policy) on every invocation.
    • --dry-run runs only the reconcile step, against the live Gateway CR, the source and destination Apache Kafka® clusters, and the cluster link, and prints the plan: each precondition (the route exists and has the expected mode, the Gateway CR is set up the way that mode needs, the cluster link mirrors from the source cluster, and spec.target.clusterId matches the destination) and a verdict for every selected topic. Nothing is changed and no migration steps run. It exits non-zero if the plan is refused. Flag overrides are applied and validated first, so a dry run rejects an invalid override exactly as a real run would. Use it to iterate on the manifest and your infrastructure before you schedule a live cutover.
  • lag-check is an interactive terminal view of replication lag for every mirror topic on the cluster link, independent of execute. It uses only the destination REST leg (spec.clusterLink.linkCredentials), so it works before execute has ever run.

Every execute reconciles the current manifest live against the cluster. A completed migration re-reconciles to nothing to do: execute then runs no migration steps and reports that. An interrupted one continues from the live state. To migrate a different topology, edit the manifest and run execute again. metadata.name is only a label (it appears in logs and the completion message). Changing it does not change what is reconciled.

Resume an interrupted migration with the same topic set (dynamic routes). On a dynamic route, kcp recognizes the fence it added by its exact shape: a rules.fencing entry with only topics (the migration's exact topic set) and blocked: true. Any other entry, including one over the same topics that also sets trafficType or topicPatterns, is an operator's, and kcp leaves it in place. If a run is interrupted after fencing, resume it with a manifest that resolves to the same topics. Resuming with a different set (a topic added or removed, or a topicPatterns entry that now also matches a topic created on the source since the interrupted run) is a different migration: kcp fences the new set, treats the earlier fence as operator-authored, and leaves it on the route, so those topics stay blocked after switchover. Finish the interrupted migration first, then migrate the changed set. If this has already happened, remove the leftover blocked entry from the route's rules.fencing by hand.

Resume an interrupted conversion. A route conversion keeps no state between runs either. kcp recognizes its conversion fence by its exact shape: a rules.fencing entry with only topicPatterns: ['.*'] and blocked: true. If a conversion is interrupted, re-run the same manifest: kcp finds its fence on the route, re-checks everything, and carries on. See Interruptions.

A static route must not carry someone else's fence. A static route has a single route-level fence. kcp recognizes its own by its exact value, {scope: ALL, errorCode: BROKER_NOT_AVAILABLE}, and refuses a route that already carries any other fence, because the switchover and a rollback would remove it: remove that fence before migrating. scope: NONE counts as no fence. An operator's plain scope: ALL fence reads back with the same defaulted errorCode, so kcp cannot tell it from its own and would remove it too. Remove it before migrating.

Each field under the declared section's policies is a default that a matching CLI flag can override for a single run, without editing the file.

docs.title: Before you run it
docs.text:
• Connections. Every execute run, including --dry-run, connects to the source Kafka cluster, the destination Kafka cluster, the cluster-link REST API, and the Kubernetes API, using the credentials and kubeconfig named in the manifest. A --dry-run only reads: on Kubernetes it reads the Gateway CR (and, for a static migration, checks that the staged Secrets exist). Every run, including a dry run, also checks that the Gateway pods serve the Gateway CR before deciding anything: it reads the CR's status, the Gateway Deployment and its pods, and, on a Gateway with hot reload on, each pod's /config endpoint. kcp refuses the run when the pods may not match the CR, and shows what it observed. The permissions to patch the Gateway and write cluster-link configurations are first used after the fence, so a real run is the first to find one missing. See Permissions.
  • Producers must use the Gateway. The fence blocks traffic that goes through the Gateway. Producers writing to the source directly are not blocked, and the check that catches them (detectUnroutedProducersDuration) is off by default. A route conversion does not use detectUnroutedProducersDuration at all. It uses its own detectUnroutedCommitsDuration check instead (see Conversion steps), which watches for consumers committing to the source directly and, like the producer check, is off by default.
  • What is fenced. A static route is fenced and switched as a whole: the topic selection only decides which mirrors are promoted and lag-checked. A dynamic route fences and switches only the selected topics.
  • Promote is the point of no return. If a step fails after the fence is up but before the promote step starts, kcp removes the fence and restores offset sync so traffic returns to the source. After promote starts, kcp never removes the fence, even if no topic was promoted yet, because doing so would split those clients from the target. The same applies from the start of a re-run that finds a topic already promoted or promoting. Fix the cause and re-run execute to roll forward. A conversion promotes nothing. Its point of no return is the switch (see Conversion steps).
  • Interrupting kcp leaves the fence up. kcp doesn't clean up when it is stopped (Ctrl+C, SIGTERM, or a crash), so the fence stays. The Gateway stays fenced until you re-run execute.
  • No deadline by default. rolloutTimeout defaults to no deadline, so a rollout that never converges waits indefinitely, with traffic already fenced.
  • A refused plan changes nothing. If reconcile refuses the plan (for example, a selected topic is not a mirror topic on the link), the whole run is refused before anything is fenced or changed. --dry-run shows the plan and the reasons.

docs.title: Migration Manifest Validation and Field Reference
docs.text: kcp validates the migration manifest every time a command reads it. This page lists the validation rules and every manifest field with its type, default, and allowed values.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Validation runs on every read of the manifest rather than through a separate kcp migration validate subcommand. Every read, by execute or lag-check, parses and structurally validates the manifest in one step, so both commands get validation automatically and neither can skip it by accident.

Validation collects every problem before returning, rather than failing fast, so you can fix the file in one pass:

3 problem(s) found in the migration manifest:
  - spec.source.bootstrapServers: must not be empty
  - spec.target.clusterId: required for target type "confluent-cloud"
  - spec.staticMigration.policies.detectUnroutedProducersDuration: must be at least 10s when set (0 skips the check) — a shorter window cannot span a producer's metadata refresh

Key rules, beyond whether each field is required or optional:

  • apiVersion and kind must be the exact literals, and metadata.name must be non-blank.
  • spec.source.type and spec.target.type must be one of their listed enum values.
  • Every bootstrapServers entry must be host:port.
  • Exactly one of spec.staticMigration, spec.dynamicMigration, and spec.dynamicToStaticConversion must be set. A manifest still using spec.route or spec.defaultPolicies is rejected with a hint to move to the new shape.
  • spec.staticMigration.consumerOffsetSync.baseline is required when pause is set, and if set at all must be enabled or disabled.
  • spec.clusterLink.name must not be blank (existence itself isn't checked until the first execute run touches the destination). spec.clusterLink.linkCredentials must not be blank.
  • Every credentials field (spec.source.credentials, spec.target.kafka.clusterCredentials, spec.clusterLink.linkCredentials) must be a non-blank file path. An inline mapping is rejected at parse.
  • spec.gateway.namespace and cr-name must not be blank. The retired crs and routes keys must not be set at all (they fail the strict decode).
  • The declared section's route.name and route.targetStreamingDomain must not be blank. A migration's topicGroup must have exactly one entry. A dynamicToStaticConversion has no topicGroup field.
  • Each entry must set at least one of topics or topicPatterns (both is allowed). Neither present is rejected. If present, topics and topicPatterns must be non-empty with no blank entries. Each topicPatterns entry must compile as an anchored RE2 regular expression.
  • Duration policies are written with a unit (0s, 10m). A bare number is a parse error.
  • No policies field can be negative. If greater than zero, detectUnroutedProducersDuration and detectUnroutedCommitsDuration must be at least 10s (0 skips the check).

Rules that need the contents of a credentials file run when that file is read, not when the manifest is parsed: the iam-needs-an-msk-source rule, the rejection of iam on the destination, and the credentials file's own validation. execute (including --dry-run) reads the source, destination, and REST credentials files. lag-check reads only the REST one.

kcp migration cutover execute --dry-run performs the same validation execute would and prints a reconcile plan, but takes no actions and runs no migration steps. It validates the manifest structure, credentials, the effective policy, and the reconcile preconditions against the live Gateway custom resource (CR), clusters, and cluster link. Use it to validate your infrastructure and manifest while you iterate, before you schedule a live cutover.

docs.title: Example: ACLs — IAM (auto-discovery)
docs.text:
Same outcome as acls-iam-explicit, but instead of naming roles individually, discoverAllRoles: true enumerates every workload IAM role in the account — AWS service-linked roles and SSO-provisioned roles are excluded automatically. Discovered grants are scoped to clusterArn: roles whose policies only grant access to other MSK clusters contribute nothing.

verifyEffectiveAccess: true simulates each discovered role's identity policies and attached permissions boundary via iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy, and keeps only the grants that are effectively allowed.

principalArns and discoverAllRoles are mutually exclusive; exactly one is required whenever spec.acls.iam is present.

The shell running kcp migration resources needs the same AWS credentials as the explicit case (iam:GetRole, iam:GetPolicy, iam:GetPolicyVersion, iam:ListRolePolicies, iam:ListAttachedRolePolicies, iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy), plus iam:GetAccountAuthorizationDetails for the account-wide enumeration.

docs.title: Credential slots
docs.text:
Slot Family This example Catalog-link spec.source.credentials Kafka IAM kafka-iam.yaml spec.target.clusterCredentials REST API key rest-api-key.yaml spec.target.cloudCredentials REST API key (distinct Cloud/Global key, same file format) rest-api-key.yaml

spec.source.credentials here only reads the MSK cluster id over IAM auth — the IAM authorization-plane reads themselves go through the AWS SDK using the shell's AWS credentials, not this file. See the credential catalog.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
kcp migration resources validate -f migration.yaml   # structural check
kcp migration resources create -f migration.yaml --dry-run   # preview, change nothing
kcp migration resources create -f migration.yaml             # migrate the ACLs

Credential paths here point at the shared catalog (../../credentials/…) to avoid duplication. For a real migration, copy the credential files next to your manifest and update the paths.

docs.title: Example: ACLs — IAM (explicit)
docs.text:
Migrates ACLs for an MSK cluster authorized via the AWS MSK IAM plane, translating a fixed list of named IAM roles. kcp migration resources reads each role's identity-based policies and translates its kafka-cluster:* grants into Confluent Cloud ACLs, scoped to clusterArn.

verifyEffectiveAccess: true simulates each role's identity policies and attached permissions boundary via iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy, and keeps only the grants that are effectively allowed.

principalArns and discoverAllRoles are mutually exclusive; exactly one is required whenever spec.acls.iam is present. This example uses principalArns — see acls-iam-discover for auto-discovery of every workload role in the account.

The shell running kcp migration resources needs AWS credentials with iam:GetRole, iam:GetPolicy, iam:GetPolicyVersion, iam:ListRolePolicies, and iam:ListAttachedRolePolicies, plus iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy for verifyEffectiveAccess.

docs.title: Example: ACLs — native
docs.text:
Migrates the source's native Kafka ACLs to Confluent Cloud, with no AWS IAM plane involved. kcp migration resources reads the source's ACLs live via DescribeAcls, resolves each distinct principal to a Confluent Cloud service account (serviceAccounts.autoCreate), and writes the matching ACLs on the target.

spec.acls alone is enough for create — no spec.clusterLink or spec.topics is required.

User:ANONYMOUS and User:* are always skipped (with a warning) unless you map them explicitly under spec.serviceAccounts.mapping; this example additionally excludes User:ANONYMOUS from spec.acls.include for clarity.

Any Kafka credential works for the source (swap in IAM, mTLS, SASL/PLAIN, …). clusterCredentials and cloudCredentials are two separate Confluent Cloud API keys — a Kafka-cluster key and a Cloud/Global key respectively — even though this example points both at the same credential file format. See the credential catalog.

docs.title: Example: ACLs — native + IAM
docs.text:
Migrates ACLs for an MSK cluster that serves both SASL/SCRAM principals and IAM roles at once. kcp migration resources reads the native Kafka ACLs (for the SASL/SCRAM principals) from the source, unions them with the IAM-derived grants (discoverAllRoles, scoped to clusterArn), deduplicates on the exact ACL tuple, and writes the result to the target.

spec.source.credentials uses SASL/SCRAM (MSK requires SCRAM-SHA-512) — this single connection both reads the source cluster id and reads the native ACLs.

spec.serviceAccounts shows an explicit mapping alongside autoCreate: the User:legacy-app principal resolves to the pre-existing sa-xxxxx service account, while every other unmapped principal (native or IAM-derived) is found-or-created via autoCreate. An explicit mapping entry always wins over autoCreate.

The shell running kcp migration resources needs AWS credentials with iam:GetRole, iam:GetPolicy, iam:GetPolicyVersion, iam:ListRolePolicies, iam:ListAttachedRolePolicies, iam:GetAccountAuthorizationDetails, and iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy for the IAM reads and verifyEffectiveAccess.

docs.title: Example: mirror topics (destination-initiated link)
docs.text:
mode: mirror creates read-only mirror topics on a cluster link, one per selected source topic, fed live through the link. It requires a spec.clusterLink. Mirror topic names are <prefix>+<sourceName> (here, msk.); with no prefix the mirror keeps the source name.

This is the destination-initiated topology (mode: destination, the default): the destination — Confluent Cloud — dials the source (MSK) to establish the link, so the source must be reachable from the destination.

docs.title: Credential slots
docs.text:
Slot Family This example Why spec.source.credentials Kafka IAM reads the MSK cluster id spec.clusterLink.source.credentials Kafka SASL/SCRAM the link dials MSK — Confluent Cloud cannot present IAM, so SCRAM spec.target.clusterCredentials REST API key Confluent Cloud Admin API

This shows three different credential files in one migration. See the full credential catalog for the other auth methods.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
kcp migration resources validate -f migration.yaml
kcp migration resources create -f migration.yaml --dry-run   # preview the link + mirror plan
kcp migration resources create -f migration.yaml             # create the link + mirror topics

An existing mirror is reported Present; a name already taken on the destination (by a plain topic, or a mirror on another link) is reported as drift and skipped — create never blindly recreates it.

docs.title: Example: new topics (no cluster link)
docs.text:
mode: new reads the source topic list and reproduces the selected topics as plain topics directly on the target — copying each source topic's partition count and explicitly-set (non-default) configs. Topics are created at the target's default replication factor (Confluent Cloud uses RF=3). It needs no cluster link, so there is no spec.clusterLink block.

create is additive: it only creates absent topics. An existing target topic whose partition count differs from the source is reported as drift and left untouched; it is never altered or deleted.

docs.title: Credential slots
docs.text:
Slot Family This example Catalog spec.source.credentials Kafka SASL/SCRAM kafka-sasl-scram.yaml spec.target.clusterCredentials REST API key rest-api-key.yaml

Any Kafka credential works for the source (swap in IAM, mTLS, SASL/PLAIN, …); any REST credential works for the target. See the credential catalog.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
kcp migration resources validate -f migration.yaml   # structural check
kcp migration resources create -f migration.yaml --dry-run   # preview, change nothing
kcp migration resources create -f migration.yaml             # create the topics

Credential paths here point at the shared catalog (../../credentials/…) to avoid duplication. For a real migration, copy the credential files next to your manifest and update the paths.

docs.title: Example: mirror topics (source-initiated link)
docs.text:
Same mode: mirror outcome as the destination-initiated example, but the link is source-initiated (mode: source). Use this when the destination cannot reach the source inbound — e.g. a private or firewalled Confluent Platform cluster. The source initiates the link outbound to the destination.

Source-initiated mode requires spec.source.type: confluent-platform (or confluent-cloud); MSK / Apache Kafka cannot initiate a link.

docs.title: How the slots differ from destination mode
docs.text:
Source mode replaces clusterLink.source with two slots:

  • sourceRest — KCP connects to the source's Admin/MDS REST to create the outbound link object.
  • destination — the source-side link's connection to the destination Kafka.
Slot Family This example Role spec.source.credentials Kafka SASL/SCRAM reads the CP cluster id spec.clusterLink.sourceRest.credentials REST Basic KCP → CP MDS (creates the link) spec.clusterLink.destination.credentials Kafka SASL/SCRAM source-side link → Confluent Cloud spec.target.clusterCredentials REST API key Confluent Cloud Admin API

See the full credential catalog for every auth method.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
kcp migration resources validate -f migration.yaml
kcp migration resources create -f migration.yaml --dry-run
kcp migration resources create -f migration.yaml

docs.title: kcp report plan — example output
docs.text:
kcp report plan turns a scan into a migration plan. For each scanned cluster it recommends a target cluster type, sizing, networking, authentication, and data-migration approach, and surfaces the questions a scan can't answer. Every run writes three artifacts: plan.md (the human-readable plan), plan.json (the same plan as structured data), and plan-inputs.yaml (the answers file you edit in place and re-run to refine the plan). The examples below show all three across the main ways the command is run.

  • filled/ — scan plus a fully answered plan-inputs.yaml. The plan is ready: 2 clusters ready to migrate, 1 routed to a specialist.
  • first-run/ — a scan with no answers yet (the seed plan-inputs.yaml from a first run). All 3 clusters need answers; the plan lists what to fill in.
  • no-scan/ — no --state-file, run as a pure questionnaire. The planner starts a single placeholder cluster, so every fact becomes a question.
  • osk-scan/ — an Apache Kafka scan (self-managed / Confluent Platform sources). The planner reads what the scan expresses (auth, partitions, tiered storage, connectors, Schema Registry) and asks for what it can't (version, source cloud).

docs.title: How these stay current
docs.text:
These examples are generated from committed fixtures, not hand-edited, so they can't silently drift from what kcp report plan actually produces:

  • demo-scan.json — the synthetic MSK scan fixture the first three examples are built from (fake account 123456789012, made-up cluster names — no real customer data).
  • demo-osk-scan.json — the synthetic Apache Kafka scan fixture the osk-scan/ example is built from (synthetic cluster, no real customer data).
  • filled-inputs.yaml — the answered plan-inputs.yaml seed used for the filled/ example. first-run/, no-scan/ and osk-scan/ start with no answers.

TestReportPlanExamples_UpToDate (in internal/services/plan/) regenerates all three artifacts for each mode through the same library entrypoints the CLI uses, normalizes the only nondeterministic bits (the plan.md Generated … timestamp and the plan.json generated_at, both fixed to <example>), and fails if the result differs from the committed files. It runs as part of make test-go.

After any change that alters plan output, regenerate with one command:

make examples

Paths in the samples are shown in relative form (demo-scan.json, plan-inputs.yaml) so they're portable. The Generated … timestamp and generated_at field carry the fixed <example> placeholder (not a real time) so the committed samples are byte-stable — expect a real timestamp on your own runs.

docs.title: Why these recommendations
docs.text:
• Cluster type: Based on your answer (private networking required), an Enterprise cluster fits: private networking starts at Enterprise, and nothing else you told us pushes it up to Dedicated. Zones: Spread across 3 Availability Zones, with a published uptime SLA up to 99.99% for this cluster type once you provision 2 or more eCKU (elastic Confluent Unit for Kafka). See the cluster-type docs for the SLA terms.
  • Sizing: Based on your scan (1,500 partitions), we size from your partition count (the only signal we have); measured ingress/egress can raise this. This tier scales with your workload, so there is no capacity for you to pick.
  • Heads up: Sizing is a lower bound; see the note at the top of the plan.
  • Networking: Based on your answer (private networking required), on AWS, we recommend PNI (Private Network Interface) for your private connection. It scales to the full 32 eCKU (elastic Confluent Unit for Kafka), so it grows with you. Confluent Cloud pulls your data over the cluster link, reaching out to your source cluster. PNI doesn't carry Cluster Linking traffic, so the link needs an Egress PrivateLink Endpoint alongside PNI.
  • Authentication: After cutover, your clients authenticate to Confluent Cloud with API keys (SASL/PLAIN). This is the default baseline; OAuth and mTLS are also available if you need them. Recreate them in Confluent Cloud: kcp create-asset migrate-acls kafka turns the ACLs from your kcp scan into Terraform, with a Confluent Cloud service account and its ACLs for each principal. Review the generated files before you apply them. Your AWS IAM policies don't carry over with your data. kcp create-asset migrate-acls iam reads the IAM policies of the roles and users you name and turns their Kafka actions into Confluent Cloud ACLs, as Terraform. It reads only the first resource in each policy statement and ignores conditions, so check each generated ACL against the policy it came from.

docs.title: Why these recommendations

• Data migration: Based on your answer (a scheduled window, all at once), we recommend a Cluster Linking cutover, moving all your clients over together in one scheduled window. Before you cut over, enable consumer offset sync on the cluster link: set consumer.offset.sync.enable=true and list the consumer groups to migrate in consumer.offset.group.filters (it defaults to none), so consumer offsets come across too. docs.title: Migration steps
docs.text:
Before you start. The steps below read these from your state file. Run any scan you haven't already, so the state file has them:

  • Schemas: kcp scan schema-registry --state-file demo-scan.json --sr-type confluent --url <source-sr-url> --use-unauthenticated (or --use-basic-auth / --use-mtls with its credentials)

Build the infrastructure this plan recommends, then move your data over it. kcp generates the Terraform for each step; you review it and terraform apply.

Step 1: create the target cluster. Create an Enterprise cluster with PNI + Egress PrivateLink Endpoint networking in the Confluent Cloud Console, or Talk to a person to set it up with a specialist. kcp create-asset target-infra isn't used here: it builds PrivateLink networking, not PNI, so it can't provision the networking this plan recommends. Set up PNI + Egress PrivateLink Endpoint networking on it and API keys (SASL/PLAIN) client authentication, and note its environment ID, cluster ID, bootstrap endpoint, and REST endpoint for the later steps. The migration link's Egress PrivateLink Endpoint is added in the link step below.

If you would rather use PrivateLink than PNI, kcp create-asset target-infra (docs) builds the environment, the cluster, and PrivateLink networking:

kcp create-asset target-infra \
  --state-file demo-scan.json \
  --source-cluster-id arn:aws:kafka:us-east-1:123456789012:cluster/clickstream/b2 \
  --needs-environment --env-name <your-env-name> \
  --needs-cluster --cluster-name <your-cluster-name> --cluster-type enterprise \
  --needs-private-link --subnet-cidrs <your-subnet-cidrs>

Step 2: prepare your source credentials. What the link needs to sign in to your source, by method:

  • AWS IAM: Nothing to do for IAM here. The cluster link uses your existing SASL/SCRAM path (above), so your MSK cluster is unchanged for the migration; your IAM clients get new Confluent Cloud credentials when you point them over. Your plan's authentication recommendation covers how to recreate your AWS IAM permissions in Confluent Cloud.
  • SASL/SCRAM: No change. Cluster Linking uses your SCRAM credentials as-is. The link's user needs READ and DESCRIBE_CONFIGS on the topics you mirror, and DESCRIBE on the consumer groups.

Step 3: build the migration link. Your data migration runs over the recommended link (Private source with external outbound cluster link (SASL/SCRAM), --type 2). Your source is private and its brokers use SASL/SCRAM, so the cluster link reaches it privately, over an external outbound endpoint, using your source's SASL/SCRAM credentials. Fill in the placeholders (the cluster you created plus a link name), then terraform apply:

kcp create-asset migration-infra \
  --type 2 \
  --source-type msk \
  --state-file demo-scan.json \
  --cluster-id arn:aws:kafka:us-east-1:123456789012:cluster/clickstream/b2 \
  --cc-type commercial \
  --target-cluster-type enterprise \
  --cluster-link-name <your-link-name> \
  --target-cluster-id <cc-cluster-id> \
  --target-rest-endpoint <cc-rest-endpoint> \
  --target-environment-id <cc-env-id>
  • <your-link-name>: a name you choose for the cluster link, for example msk-to-cc.
  • <cc-env-id>, <cc-cluster-id>, <cc-rest-endpoint>: from the cluster you created.

Alternative: a jump cluster in your VPC (SASL/SCRAM), if Confluent Cloud can't reach your brokers over an egress endpoint. That is --type 4, which needs extra jump-cluster inputs (a bootstrap endpoint, an existing PrivateLink endpoint, and subnet CIDRs). See the docs.

Step 4: create your topics on the target. Recreate your source topics as mirror topics that the cluster link forwards your data into, with their partition counts and configs, using kcp create-asset migrate-topics (docs):

kcp create-asset migrate-topics \
  --mode mirror \
  --source-type msk \
  --state-file demo-scan.json \
  --cluster-id arn:aws:kafka:us-east-1:123456789012:cluster/clickstream/b2 \
  --cc-type commercial \
  --target-cluster-id <cc-cluster-id> \
  --target-rest-endpoint <cc-rest-endpoint> \
  --cluster-link-name <your-link-name>

Step 5: migrate your schemas. Copy the source schemas into Confluent Cloud Schema Registry; the Schema recommendation above covers the approach. Run kcp create-asset migrate-schemas (docs):

kcp create-asset migrate-schemas \
  --url <source-sr-url> \
  --state-file demo-scan.json \
  --cc-type commercial \
  --cc-sr-rest-endpoint <cc-sr-rest-endpoint>

Step 6: run the cutover. Before you cut over, enable consumer offset sync on the cluster link: set consumer.offset.sync.enable=true and list the consumer groups to migrate in consumer.offset.group.filters (it defaults to none), so consumer offsets come across too. In the properties file, set consumer.offset.sync.enable=true and consumer.offset.group.filters={"groupFilters":[{"name":"<consumer-group>","patternType":"LITERAL","filterType":"INCLUDE"}]}. Then run confluent kafka link configuration update <your-link-name> --config <your-link-config-file> (docs). At cutover, stop your producers and consumers, wait for the mirror to catch up (lag zero) and one consumer offset sync interval, promote the mirror topics so they accept writes, then restart your clients against Confluent Cloud.

What changes for each client app at cutover: point it at the new Confluent Cloud bootstrap endpoint; switch its security config to API keys (SASL/PLAIN) with the new Confluent Cloud credentials; and, for any app that uses Schema Registry, point it at the new Confluent Cloud Schema Registry URL.

At cutover, stop the schema exporter and set the Confluent Cloud Schema Registry back to READWRITE, so producers can register new schemas.

Backing out: until you promote the mirror topics, nothing is committed: your source keeps taking writes until you stop your producers and cut over. To roll back, restart your producers against the still-running source instead of promoting the mirror.

Step 7: decommission. Delete the cluster link and the Egress PrivateLink Endpoint, then retire your source cluster.

Access control (set up separately). Your source's authorization rules don't carry over. Recreate them with kcp create-asset migrate-acls iam and kcp create-asset migrate-acls kafka. The Authentication recommendation above covers what it reads. Do this before cutover. This is independent of moving your data — plan it alongside the steps above, not after.

docs.title: Migration steps
docs.text:
Before you start. The steps below read these from your state file. Run any scan you haven't already, so the state file has them:

  • Schemas: kcp scan schema-registry --state-file demo-scan.json --sr-type glue --registry-name <glue-registry-name> --region <glue-region>

Your data moves with Confluent Replicator, because Cluster Linking needs an Enterprise or Dedicated cluster. Create the cluster and its structure, run Replicator, then cut over.

Step 1: create the target cluster. Create a Standard cluster with Public endpoint networking in the Confluent Cloud Console. (kcp create-asset target-infra provisions Enterprise and Dedicated clusters only.) Set up API keys (SASL/PLAIN) client authentication on it, and note its cluster ID, bootstrap endpoint, and REST endpoint for the later steps.

Step 2: create your topics on the target. Recreate your source topics as plain topics on the new cluster (no data yet), with their partition counts and configs, using kcp create-asset migrate-topics (docs):

kcp create-asset migrate-topics \
  --mode new \
  --source-type msk \
  --state-file demo-scan.json \
  --cluster-id arn:aws:kafka:us-west-2:123456789012:cluster/logs-ingest/c3 \
  --cc-type commercial \
  --target-cluster-id <cc-cluster-id> \
  --target-rest-endpoint <cc-rest-endpoint>

Step 3: migrate your schemas. Copy the source schemas into Confluent Cloud Schema Registry; the Schema recommendation above covers the approach. Run kcp create-asset migrate-schemas (docs):

kcp create-asset migrate-schemas \
  --glue-registry <glue-registry-name> \
  --state-file demo-scan.json \
  --cc-type commercial \
  --cc-sr-rest-endpoint <cc-sr-rest-endpoint>

Step 4: copy your data with Confluent Replicator. Run Confluent Replicator on a Kafka Connect worker in your own account to copy data from your source into the new cluster (docs). It reads your source with your existing credentials and writes into Confluent Cloud with the target credentials (the client authentication) you set up in Step 1, and it needs a Confluent Platform Enterprise license.

Step 5: cut over. Once Replicator has caught up, move your clients to Confluent Cloud. Consumer offsets don't carry over on their own: translate them with the Confluent timestamp interceptor, added to every consumer before you start (Java clients only) (docs). Non-Java consumers have no automatic offset-translation path here — they resume according to each consumer's auto.offset.reset (reprocessing from earliest, or skipping to latest), so plan their cutover accordingly.

What changes for each client app at cutover: point it at the new Confluent Cloud bootstrap endpoint; switch its security config to API keys (SASL/PLAIN) with the new Confluent Cloud credentials; and, for any app that uses Schema Registry, point it at the new Confluent Cloud Schema Registry URL.

At cutover, switch your clients from the AWS Glue Schema Registry serializers to Confluent Schema Registry serializers. Messages already mirrored keep their Glue format, so consumers that read that history still need the Glue deserializer.

Backing out: your source keeps taking writes and serving your applications until you move the clients, so nothing is committed before cutover. To roll back, leave your clients pointed at the still-running source (or point them back to it) instead of completing the move.

Step 6: decommission. Stop Replicator and its Connect worker, then retire your source cluster.

Access control (set up separately). Your source's authorization rules don't carry over. Recreate them with kcp create-asset migrate-acls kafka. The Authentication recommendation above covers what it reads. Do this before cutover. This is independent of moving your data — plan it alongside the steps above, not after.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Every question, its wording, and its options, listed once. Set answers per cluster (or fleet-wide in all_clusters:) in plan-inputs.yaml; see Answers by cluster for each cluster's current answers and what's still needed.

Key Question Options use_case_breadth How widely is this cluster used? one-app → One team, one applicationfew-teams → A few teams or applicationsshared-fabric → Shared fabric across many apps and teams move_existing_data Do you need to move your existing data? true → Yes, move my existing data: Brings your history along. Availability depends on your source setup.false → No, we can start fresh: Moves producers to the new cluster first, then consumers once they finish the old one private_networking_required Is private networking a hard requirement?Answer based on your requirement, not your current setup. Public endpoints on Confluent Cloud are authenticated and encrypted. true → Yes, private networking is requiredfalse → No, public endpoints are fine connects_today How do you connect to your cluster today? same-vpc → Same VPCpeered → Peeredprivatelink → PrivateLinkother → Other or more than one cc_egress_required Will any of Confluent Cloud's managed connectors or consumers need to connect into your private network?For example, a connector writing to a private database, or a managed Confluent component calling a private API inside your network. true → Yesfalse → No schema_registry What Schema Registry does your source environment use? none → None: Schemaless, or schemas kept in app codeglue → AWS Glue Schema Registrycp-enterprise-7.1 → Confluent Schema Registry: Enterprise, 7.1 or later: Confluent Platform Enterprise, version 7.1 or latercp-community → Confluent Schema Registry: Community, or below 7.1: Community edition, or Confluent Platform below version 7.1other → Other, not sure schema_strategy What do you want to do with your schemas on Confluent Cloud? migrate → Migrate my existing schemasfresh → Start fresh on Confluent Cloudschemaless → Stay schemaless downtime_tolerance What is your target downtime window at cutover? window-all → A scheduled window, all at oncewindow-sequential → A scheduled window, one service at a timeminutes → Minutes per serviceseconds → Seconds per servicezero → Zero downtime exceeds_standard_limits Does your workload exceed any of the following: 250 megabytes/sec ingress, 750 megabytes/sec egress, or 15,000 requests/sec?If you exceed any of these, we'll plan for an Enterprise cluster instead of Standard. Enterprise runs on private networking. true → Yesfalse → No (default) exceeds_enterprise_limits Does your workload exceed any of the following: 1,920 megabytes/sec ingress, 5,760 megabytes/sec egress, or 240,000 requests/sec? true → Yesfalse → No (default) target_cloud Which cloud should your new Confluent Cloud cluster run on?This is independent of your source cloud. Confluent supports cross-cloud migrations. aws → AWS (default)azure → Azuregcp → GCP target_auth Which authentication methods should your Confluent Cloud cluster support? Select all that apply.A cluster can support several at once. On AWS and Azure we keep your existing mTLS as-is; on Google Cloud, mTLS needs a Dedicated cluster, which we plan with you. OAuth and API keys are always set up new. api-keys → API keys (SASL/PLAIN)oauth → OAuthmtls → mTLSSelect all that apply, as a list, for example [api-keys, oauth]. client_coordination How much coordination will it take to cut over all your clients and apps at the same time? easy → Low (few clients, one team)moderate → Moderate (default)hard → High (many clients and teams) eos_streams Do any applications use exactly-once transactions and/or Kafka Streams? eos → Exactly-once or transactionskstreams → Kafka StreamsSelect all that apply, as a list, for example [eos, kstreams]. consumer_history_requirement Do your consumers need historical data available after migration?Only relevant when there's history to carry (tiered storage or long retention) and you're moving existing data. true → Yes (default)false → No source_cluster_type Source cluster type provisioned → Provisionedserverless → Serverless kafka_version What Kafka version does your source cluster run?Below Kafka 2.4, Cluster Linking isn't available, so we use Confluent Replicator instead. 3.0-plus → 3.0 or newer2.4-2.9 → 2.4–2.9older → Older than 2.4 inter_broker_protocol Is your inter-broker protocol (IBP) 2.8 or later?This only matters when your Kafka version is 2.4–2.9. An inter-broker protocol below 2.8 blocks Cluster Linking even if your Kafka version qualifies. true → Yes, 2.8 or laterfalse → No, below 2.8 source_auth How your Kafka clients authenticate today iam → AWS IAMscram → SASL/SCRAMmtls → TLS client certificates (mTLS)unauth → None / plaintextSelect all that apply, as a list, for example [iam, scram]. tiered_storage Do your topics use tiered storage?Tiered data is stored separately from your active topics, in Amazon S3, so retrieving it during cutover takes extra time and can add cost. true → Yesfalse → No topics_have_custom_settings Do any of your topics use non-default settings?This includes retention over 7 days, a replication factor other than 3, a max message size over 2 MB, or a cleanup policy that combines compact and delete. true → Yesfalse → No msk_connect_present Do you use MSK Connect? true → Yesfalse → No self_managed_connectors Do you run self-managed Kafka Connect? true → Yesfalse → No

docs.title: Migrate Consumer Groups
docs.text:
This guide explains how consumer groups move to Confluent Cloud on each Confluent Gateway migration type, what to check before you start, what your consumers see during the switch, and how to confirm the groups came across intact.

A consumer group is more than its members. It is a set of committed offsets, one per partition it reads, and a group coordinator, the broker that tracks who is in the group and who owns which partition. Moving a group to Confluent Cloud means moving both: the committed offsets have to reach the destination so the group resumes where it stopped, and the coordinator has to move so its members can commit and rebalance there. A cutover through the Gateway does this without changing any client configuration. Which mechanism does the work depends on the route.

This guide builds on Migrate with a static route, Migrate with a dynamic route, and Convert a dynamic route to static, which cover the mechanics of each cutover.

docs.title: How groups move
docs.text:
Static migration Dynamic migration Conversion Committed offsets reach the destination The cluster link syncs them ahead of the switch They don't. Groups keep committing to the source kcp copies them itself, during the conversion Group coordinator moves At the switch Stays on the source At the switch Link's consumer.offset.sync.enable On. kcp doesn't check Off. kcp refuses otherwise Off. kcp refuses otherwise Which groups The groups the link's consumer.offset.group.filters selects Every group on the route, coordinated by the source Groups whose committed offsets are all on the link's topics KIP-848 consumers (group.protocol=consumer) Supported Not supported Supported after the route is static

Consumer groups on a dynamic route are a stage, not a destination. A topic-based migration moves topics, and the groups keep working because the source still coordinates them. The groups themselves only move when you convert the route to static. If you'd rather move groups in one step, use a static migration.

docs.title: Prerequisites and limitations
docs.text:
All route types

  • Every member of every group connects through the Gateway. A member that connects to the source directly while the rest of the group connects through the route splits the group across two coordinators, and both halves can process the same partitions. The fence can't block a client that bypasses the Gateway, so stop such clients and restart them on the route. A member that reaches the source through another route on the Gateway counts the same way. kcp migrates one route per run, so after this route moves, that member is on a different coordinator. Move every member of a group onto the route before you migrate it.
  • Every topic a group has committed offsets on is a mirror topic on the cluster link. Offsets are only ever synced or copied for the link's topics, because the destination rejects offset commits for a topic it doesn't have.
  • Consumers can reach the destination with the credentials they use today, and have READ on their groups and topics there.

Static migration

  • Consumer offset sync is on for the link, and consumer.offset.group.filters includes every group you are moving. The Confluent default for the filter is no groups. A link created with kcp migration resources create defaults to an include-all filter when sync is on.
  • kcp doesn't check either setting for a static route. A group that isn't in the filter has no committed offsets on the destination, and its consumers start from auto.offset.reset there.
  • No consumer of a group you are moving runs against the destination before the cutover. The cluster link can overwrite the destination's offsets for a filtered group that is used there, and a group that is active on the destination can leave a mirror topic stuck in PENDING_MIRROR during promote. Setting consumerOffsetSync.pause: true disables offset sync before promote, which avoids the stuck mirror. See Migrate from a non-Confluent cluster to Confluent Cloud.

Dynamic migration and conversion

  • The cluster link's consumer offset sync is off, and the route's rules.routing.coordination.group is the source. kcp refuses both a link with sync on and a route that doesn't pin coordination to the source.
  • Consumers use the classic group protocol. A consumer with group.protocol=consumer can't start against a dynamic route.
  • Share groups aren't supported on a dynamic route.
  • The cluster link and the source topics stay until the conversion is done. While the route is dynamic, committed offsets for migrated topics are still stored on the source, and the source rejects commits for a topic it no longer has. The conversion also reads the link to decide which groups are in scope. See Convert a dynamic route to static.

kcp keeps group coordination on the source

The Gateway can coordinate groups on the destination for the whole life of a dynamic migration, by setting coordination.group to the destination. kcp doesn't run migrations that way. It pins coordination to the source and moves it once, in the conversion. For the Gateway's own sequence, see Migrate Topics Incrementally with Topic-Based Routing and Fencing.

Cluster link permissions

The link reads the source with the credential it was created with. It needs READ, DESCRIBE, and DESCRIBE_CONFIGS on the topics you mirror, and with offset sync on, READ and DESCRIBE on the consumer groups it syncs. An MSK link uses SCRAM because a cluster link can't use IAM credentials, so these are Apache Kafka® access control lists (ACLs) on MSK. See Permissions.

docs.title: Audit your groups
docs.text:
Before you choose a route or write a manifest, list what you have. List every group on the source and the topics each commits on:

kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server <source_bootstrap> --command-config source.properties --describe --all-groups

Look for:

  • Groups that commit on topics outside the migration. On a conversion, a group with any committed offset on a topic that isn't on the link refuses the run. On a static migration those offsets are never synced.
  • Groups with members outside the Gateway. Find them before the fence does. A consumer that bypasses the Gateway keeps committing to the source after the switch.
  • Empty and stale groups. A group with no members still has committed offsets, and is in scope. Delete groups nobody owns, or their stale offsets, rather than carry them across.
  • Groups that already exist on the destination. A conversion refuses an in-scope group with live members on the destination, and warns about one without members because its offsets are overwritten. On a static migration, look yourself.

docs.title: Move groups with a static migration
docs.text: On a static route the cluster link carries the committed offsets. The link syncs them from the source to the destination continuously, so by the time you cut over the destination already holds recent offsets for every group in the filter. The switch moves the coordinator, and the consumers pick up from the synced offsets.

docs.title: Prepare the link
docs.text:
You configure offset sync on the link, not in the migration manifest:

  • consumer.offset.sync.enable=true
  • consumer.offset.group.filters, a JSON filter naming the groups to sync. Each entry has a name, a patternType (LITERAL or PREFIXED), and a filterType (INCLUDE or EXCLUDE).
  • consumer.offset.sync.ms, how often offsets sync. The default is 30 seconds, and it can go as low as 1 second. A shorter interval keeps the destination's offsets fresher, at the cost of some link throughput.
{
  "groupFilters": [
    { "name": "*", "patternType": "LITERAL", "filterType": "INCLUDE" }
  ]
}

Sync is asynchronous, so the destination's offsets always trail the source's by up to one interval. Anything a consumer processed since the last sync is read again after the switch. See What your consumers see.

To check offset sync is working before the window, describe a group on the destination twice, one sync interval apart, while it consumes on the source. Its committed offsets should move. The commands are in After the cutover.

docs.title: What the cutover does with offset sync
docs.text:
The cutover's stages are the same as for any static migration. Two of them are about offsets:

  1. Fence. Clients can no longer commit. The source's committed offsets stop moving.
  2. Pause offset sync (optional). kcp waits consumerOffsetSyncDrainDuration, so the link runs further sync cycles and carries the final committed offsets across, then disables the link's offset sync.
  3. After the switch, kcp restores the link's offset sync to your consumerOffsetSync.baseline.

Set the drain to at least two of the link's sync intervals, so at least one full cycle completes after the fence. Draining narrows the re-read window but can't close it: sync is asynchronous, so a drain reduces duplicates and doesn't guarantee none.

staticMigration:
  # route and topicGroup as in the static guide
  consumerOffsetSync:
    pause: true
    baseline: enabled
  policies:
    consumerOffsetSyncDrainDuration: 60s # two sync intervals at the 30s default

Pausing is optional. It stops the link writing offsets to the destination from immediately before promote, which matters in two cases. A group whose consumers commit on the destination while the link still syncs it would have those commits overwritten. And a group already active on the destination can leave a mirror topic stuck during promote. If either could apply to your groups, turn it on. The drain runs while the route is fenced, so it lengthens the pause clients see rather than shortening it.

Pausing clears the link's group filters

Disabling consumer.offset.sync.enable clears consumer.offset.group.filters on the link, and the restore sets only consumer.offset.sync.enable back to your baseline. Because kcp keeps no state between runs, it has no record of the filters to put back. After a pause the link is enabled with an empty filter. This has no effect on the migration, because offset sync stops for every promoted mirror topic. It only matters if you reuse the link afterward while it still has unpromoted mirror topics. In that case, set the filter again yourself.

For a manual alternative that needs no pause, the Cluster Linking migration guide stops the consumers on the source, waits at least one consumer.offset.sync.ms, removes their group from the filter, checks the offsets arrived, and restarts them on the destination.

If a run stops before promote, kcp removes the fence and restores offset sync, as for any static migration. See If a run stops.

docs.title: Groups on a dynamic route
docs.text:
A topic-based migration doesn't move groups. The route's coordination stays pinned to the source, the link's offset sync stays off, and each batch moves topics only. After a batch switches:

  • The batch's consumers read the migrated topics from Confluent Cloud, through the route.
  • Their groups still commit to the source, because the source coordinates every group on the route. Offsets are portable here because a mirror topic preserves the source's offsets, so a position committed on the source is the right position on the destination.

Nothing about consumer groups changes between batches, and the batch manifest has no consumer group settings. Three things behave differently while the route is dynamic:

  • kafka-consumer-groups and other tools that call the group admin APIs don't work against the route. Point them at the source directly to inspect a group.
  • Every member of a group has to use the route, as above.
  • KIP-848 consumers can't connect at all. They come onto the route after the conversion.

The groups move when you convert.

docs.title: Move groups during a conversion
docs.text:
A conversion closes out a topic-based migration. kcp fences every topic on the route, checks that no client is still committing to the source directly, copies each in-scope group's committed offsets to the destination, and switches the route to a static route bound to the destination. The coordinator moves with the switch.

For the full scope and every check kcp makes, see Convert a dynamic route to static. For consumer groups:

  • Scope. The cluster link. A group whose committed offsets are all on link topics is copied.
  • Refusals. A group with a committed offset on a topic that isn't on the link, and an in-scope group with members on the destination. See Refusals.
  • Direct commits. kcp takes two snapshots of every source group's committed offsets, detectUnroutedCommitsDuration apart. If any changed, a consumer commits to the source directly, and kcp unfences the route and stops. You can't turn off this check.
  • Offset sync. kcp refuses if the offsets in the sync are past a destination partition's high-water mark. You don't turn link offset sync back on for a conversion.
  • Permissions. kcp's destination credential needs READ on every group and topic to write their offsets. See Permissions.

docs.title: What your consumers see
docs.text:
All three paths share one client experience at the switch.

  • A pause. From the fence to the switch, consumers on the route fetch nothing and can't commit. A static migration pauses the whole route. A dynamic batch pauses only the batch's topics. A conversion pauses the whole route for about detectUnroutedCommitsDuration plus two Gateway reloads.
  • A rejoin. After the switch the coordinator is on the destination, which doesn't know the consumers' members. Each consumer's first commit or heartbeat there fails, so it rejoins its group and resumes from the destination's committed offset. Consumers handle this in the client library. No configuration changes.
  • Possibly a re-read. A consumer re-reads whatever it processed after the last committed offset the destination holds. On a static migration that is bounded by the sync interval and the drain. On a conversion it is up to one poll for a consumer that commits after every batch, and up to the backlog the fence built for one that auto-commits. Nothing is skipped. Design consumers to be idempotent, as you would for any at-least-once consumer.

docs.title: After the cutover
docs.text:
Confirm the groups, not only that consumers reconnected:

  • Members rejoined their groups on Confluent Cloud, and each group is Stable.
  • Each group's committed offsets on the destination match the source's last offsets for the same partitions, and the group's lag is falling.
  • No group has members on both clusters.
  • If you paused offset sync, the link is back at your consumerOffsetSync.baseline.

Compare a group on both clusters:

kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server <source_bootstrap> --command-config source.properties --describe --group <group>
kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server <destination_bootstrap> --command-config destination.properties --describe --group <group>

Both commands work against Confluent Cloud, with a cluster API key in destination.properties.

After promote starts, or after the switch for a conversion, a migration only moves forward. kcp doesn't move clients back to the source after that point, so validate with --dry-run and lag-check before the window.

docs.title: Migrate With a Dynamic Gateway Route
docs.text:
A dynamic migration moves topics to Confluent Cloud in batches, with no client configuration changes.

Your applications already connect to the Confluent Gateway. A dynamic route binds both the source and the destination and sends each topic to one or the other according to routing rules. Cutting over a batch means fencing only those topics, promoting their mirror topics on the cluster link, and adding a routing rule that sends them to the destination. Clients reconnect to the same Gateway address, and everything outside the batch keeps flowing to the source.

This guide walks through the prerequisites, the migration manifest, and a batch run. For how dynamic migrations compare with static ones, see Gateway migrations.

Early Access

Dynamic routing is an Early Access feature of Confluent Private Cloud Gateway 1.4, intended for evaluation and non-production testing. Its configuration schema might change before general availability. Before you plan a migration, read Migrate Topics Incrementally with Topic-Based Routing and Fencing.

docs.title: Prerequisites and limitations
docs.text:
Gateway

  • The Gateway runs on Kubernetes and is managed by Confluent for Kubernetes (CFK). kcp reads and patches the Gateway custom resource (CR), so a Gateway started any other way can't be migrated.
  • The route to migrate is dynamic: it binds exactly two streaming domains, the source and the destination, and sets rules.routing.coordination.group to the source.
  • The route uses the host broker identification strategy, which requires TLS between clients and the Gateway. kcp doesn't check this. The Gateway rejects a dynamic route that doesn't.
  • The destination is one of the two bound domains, and the route already carries security.cluster.<domain> authentication for both. PLAIN and OAUTHBEARER are supported on a dynamic route, but SCRAM is not.
  • kcp adds and removes its own fence and routing rules in rules. Any fence or routing rule you authored stays in place. See If a run stops.
  • Gateway 1.4.0 and later, and CFK 3.4.0 and later. See Version requirements.

Cluster link

  • A cluster link from the source to the destination already exists, and every topic you select is a mirror topic on it. kcp migration cutover never creates either. To set them up, use kcp migration resources create.
  • A dynamic route uses one cluster link. Every batch on the route migrates over that link, and the later conversion uses it to decide which topics and consumer groups to move. spec.clusterLink takes a single link, and kcp doesn't check whether another manifest names a different link for the same route. Don't spread one route's batches across several links: topics on the others fall outside the conversion's scope, and a consumer group that commits on one of them refuses the conversion. Add every batch's topics to the same link instead.
  • If you plan to convert the route to static afterward, keep the cluster link and the source topics until the conversion is done, and create the link without a cluster.link.prefix. The conversion reads the link to find what to move, copies consumer group offsets from the source topics, and refuses a link whose mirrors are named differently on the destination.
  • Consumer offset sync must be off for the link. kcp refuses to run otherwise. Consumer groups stay coordinated by the source while the route is dynamic, so the link has no offsets to sync for them. kcp migration resources create turns offset sync on by default. To create the link with sync off, set consumerOffsetSync.enable: false in its manifest. For an existing link, set consumer.offset.sync.enable=false in the link's configuration.
  • Mirror lag must be at or below lagThreshold (default 0, fully caught up) before kcp fences the batch. After the fence, kcp waits for each mirror to reach exactly zero lag before it promotes.

Clients

  • Every producer and consumer connects through the Gateway. The fence only blocks traffic that goes through it, so a producer writing to the source directly keeps writing.
  • Producers use acks=1 or acks=all. Fenced clients get an error they can retry, and they buffer in the meantime. With acks=0, producers never see the error, and their records are dropped.
  • Consumers use the classic group protocol. KIP-848 consumers (group.protocol=consumer) can't use a dynamic route at all, for the whole life of the migration.
  • Every member of a consumer group connects through the route, or the group splits across two coordinators.
  • Transactional workloads and share groups aren't supported on a dynamic route.

Limitations

  • Only the topics in the batch are fenced and switched. Everything else on the route is untouched.
  • A manifest migrates one route and one topic group per run, so each batch is its own manifest. Batches must contain disjoint topics.
  • The point of no return is the start of promote. After it, kcp never rolls back. A failure leaves the batch's fence up until you re-run and the batch completes.
  • Ctrl+C leaves the fence in place. Re-run execute to continue.
  • Topic auto-creation isn't supported on a dynamic route, and some consumer group admin APIs are unavailable, so tools such as kafka-consumer-groups don't work against it.
  • A migration leaves the route dynamic. Finish the job with a conversion.
  • Create the cluster link without cluster.link.prefix. kcp expects each mirror topic to have the same name on both clusters.
  • Cutover doesn't migrate schemas. Move them before the cutover, for example with kcp iac schemas generate.

Access

  • Credentials for the source, the destination Apache Kafka® listener, and the cluster link REST API, each as a credentials file.
  • A Kubernetes identity that can read and patch the Gateway CR, read its Deployment, and list its pods. With hot reload on, it also needs get on pods/proxy and a cluster-scoped get on the Gateway custom resource definition (CRD). For the full Role, see Permissions.

docs.title: How a batch cutover works
docs.text:
kcp keeps no state between runs. Each run reconciles the manifest against the live Gateway, both clusters, and the cluster link, and continues from wherever they already are. For one batch on a dynamic route the stages are:

  1. Check lag. Every topic in the batch must be within lagThreshold. Nothing is fenced yet, so kcp waits for it.
  2. Fence. kcp adds a rules.fencing entry that blocks the batch's topics (blocked: true) and waits for every Gateway pod to apply it. Clients of those topics get errors they can retry, and they buffer in the meantime.
  3. Verify the fence. If detectUnroutedProducersDuration is set, kcp reads the source's partition offsets for the batch's topics, waits that duration, and reads them again. If any offset advanced, a producer is still writing to the source directly, and kcp aborts and unfences the batch instead of promoting.
  4. Promote. kcp waits for each mirror to reach zero lag, then promotes the mirror topics in batches of promoteBatchSize and waits for each to stop mirroring. This is the point of no return.
  5. Switch. In a single update to the route's rules, kcp adds a routing condition that sends the batch's topics to the destination and removes its fence. Clients reconnect to the same Gateway address and land on Confluent Cloud.

A dynamic migration has no offset sync stage: the link's consumer offset sync is already off, and kcp neither pauses nor restores it.

At the fence step, before the first change that blocks traffic, kcp works out how the Gateway applies a new configuration: in place (hot reload) or by rolling its pods. With hot reload, it proves the Gateway applies a configuration revision before anything is blocked, and refuses if it can't. This happens after the lag wait and not under --dry-run. Then it waits for every pod to confirm each change. rolloutTimeout and hotReloadTimeout bound those waits.

A failure before promote removes the fence, so the batch's traffic returns to the source.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the dynamic route on the Gateway
docs.text:
The route binds both clusters from the start. Before the first batch, every topic is routed to the source, and the fencing list is empty. This is the part of the CR that matters for a dynamic migration. The rest is your normal Gateway configuration.

apiVersion: platform.confluent.io/v1beta1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: gateway-initial
  namespace: confluent
spec:
  secretStores:
    - name: file-store
      # ...
  streamingDomains:
    - name: source-kafka-cluster
      type: kafka
      kafkaCluster:
        bootstrapServers:
          - id: UNAUTHED
            endpoint: PLAINTEXT://source-kafka.confluent.svc.cluster.local:9071
    - name: confluent-cloud
      type: kafka
      kafkaCluster:
        bootstrapServers:
          - id: SASL_PLAIN
            endpoint: SASL_SSL://pkc-xxxxx.us-east-1.aws.confluent.cloud:9092
            tls:
              secretRef: tls
  routes:
    - name: migration-route
      endpoint: bootstrap.gw.example.local:9595
      # Dynamic routes require the host strategy, and with it client TLS.
      brokerIdentificationStrategy:
        type: host
        pattern: "broker$(nodeId).gw.example.local"
      mode: dynamic
      # Plural streamingDomains also makes this a dynamic route.
      streamingDomains:
        - name: source-kafka-cluster
          bootstrapServerId: UNAUTHED
        - name: confluent-cloud
          bootstrapServerId: SASL_PLAIN
      rules:
        routing:
          coordination:
            # Pinned to the source for the life of the migration.
            group: source-kafka-cluster
          # Topics that match no condition go here. Every topic starts on the
          # source; kcp adds a condition per migrated batch.
          default: source-kafka-cluster
        fencing: []
      security:
        client:
          authentication:
            type: none
          tls:
            secretRef: client-tls
        cluster:
          # Every bound domain needs an entry.
          source-kafka-cluster:
            auth: passthrough
          confluent-cloud:
            auth: swap
            secretStore: file-store
            authentication:
              type: plain
              jaasConfigPassThrough:
                secretRef: plain-jaas

kcp checks the route on every run, before anything is fenced, and --dry-run reports it. It needs exactly two bound domains, coordination.group set to the source, and the manifest's targetStreamingDomain to be one of the two. Routing conditions must compile as anchored full-match regular expressions.

To build the route yourself, see the CFK documentation for routes, routing rules, authentication swapping, and secret stores. See also Migrate Topics with Topic-Based Routing.

docs.title: 2. Plan the batches
docs.text:
Each batch is a manifest with its own topic group. Choose batches so that:

  • Topics that must move together are in the same batch. Find them before you plan. The transactional workloads guide shows how, though transactional workloads themselves need a static migration.
  • Batches are disjoint. A topic already migrated by an earlier batch is skipped (nothing to do), so overlap doesn't fail, but it isn't a way to re-run a batch.
  • Every consumer of a topic in the batch is ready for the pause. Consumers and producers of those topics are blocked from the fence until the switch. All other topics keep running.

docs.title: 3. Write the migration manifest
docs.text:
The manifest declares the migration with spec.dynamicMigration. Everything outside that section is the same as in a static migration. Every credentials field is a path to a credentials file, and the manifest holds no secrets. Paths resolve relative to the working directory you run kcp from.

apiVersion: kcp.confluent.io/v1alpha1
kind: GatewayMigration

metadata:
  name: msk-prod-to-cc-batch-1

spec:
  source:
    type: msk # msk | apache-kafka
    bootstrapServers:
      - b-1.msk-prod.abc123.c2.kafka.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:9096
    credentials: /etc/kcp/source-creds.yaml

  target:
    type: confluent-cloud # confluent-cloud | confluent-platform
    clusterId: lkc-abc123
    kafka:
      bootstrapServers:
        - pkc-xxxxx.us-east-1.aws.confluent.cloud:9092
      restEndpoint: https://pkc-xxxxx.us-east-1.aws.confluent.cloud:443
      clusterCredentials: /etc/kcp/dest-kafka-creds.yaml

  clusterLink:
    name: msk-to-cc # must already exist on the destination
    linkCredentials: /etc/kcp/link-creds.yaml

  gateway:
    namespace: confluent
    cr-name: gateway-initial

  dynamicMigration:
    route:
      name: migration-route # the dynamic route in the Gateway CR
      targetStreamingDomain: confluent-cloud # one of the two domains the route binds
    # This batch only. Later batches are separate manifests with disjoint topics.
    topicGroup:
      - topics: ["t1.order", "t1.inventory"]
        # topicPatterns: ['t1\..*'] # RE2, matched against the full topic name. Resolved against the live source on every run.
    policies:
      lagThreshold: 0
      promoteBatchSize: 100
      rolloutTimeout: 10m
      detectUnroutedProducersDuration: 30s # 0s skips the check; minimum 10s
      hotReloadTimeout: 90s

Notes on the choices above:

  • The manifest has no consumerOffsetSync block. It is static-only, because a dynamic route needs offset sync off.
  • topicGroup takes literal topics, anchored topicPatterns, or both (the union), and has no default.
  • Patterns are resolved against the source on every run. A topic created since an interrupted run can change the batch, and kcp then treats the earlier fence as someone else's. Prefer literal topics for a batch you might need to resume, or finish the interrupted batch first.
  • detectUnroutedProducersDuration is off by default. If you can't rule out producers bypassing the Gateway, turn it on.
  • rolloutTimeout defaults to no deadline, so a rollout that never converges waits indefinitely with traffic already fenced. Set one.

The complete annotated manifest is gateway-dynamic-migration.yaml. Every field, validation rule, and policy default is in the migration manifest reference.

docs.title: 4. Dry run
docs.text:
kcp migration cutover execute --migration-yaml migration.yaml --dry-run

A dry run validates the manifest and credentials, then reads the live Gateway CR, both clusters, and the cluster link, and prints the plan: each route check and a verdict per topic. It changes nothing and exits non-zero if the plan is refused. Run it until it passes.

A run is refused, with nothing changed, when any of the following is true:

  • The route isn't dynamic, doesn't bind exactly two domains, doesn't bind the target, or doesn't pin coordination.group to the source.
  • Consumer offset sync is still enabled on the cluster link.
  • The cluster link doesn't mirror from spec.source, or spec.target.clusterId doesn't match the destination.
  • A selected topic isn't on the source, isn't on the cluster link, exists on the destination without being a mirror, or has a mirror in a failed or paused state.

docs.title: 5. Watch the lag
docs.text:
kcp migration cutover lag-check --migration-yaml migration.yaml

lag-check shows replication lag for every mirror topic on the link, whatever the topic selection. It only needs the link REST credentials, so you can run it long before the cutover.

docs.title: Run a batch
docs.text:
Schedule a window for the batch's applications. Their clients are paused from the fence until the switch.

kcp migration cutover execute --migration-yaml migration.yaml

You can override any policy for a single run with its flag, for example --detect-unrouted-producers-duration 60s. See the command reference.

When it finishes, kcp prints Migration completed: <metadata.name>. Re-running a completed batch reconciles to nothing to do.

docs.title: If a run stops
docs.text:
Where it stopped What happened What to do Before the fence (refused plan, lag above threshold) Nothing was changed. Fix the cause and re-run. After the fence, before promote (for example unrouted producer) kcp removes the fence. The batch's traffic returns to the source. The exit is non-zero. Fix the cause (for example reconfigure the producer) and re-run. During or after promote The fence stays. Rolling back would split promoted topics from their clients. Fix the cause and re-run execute. It rolls forward. Switch reached the CR but wasn't confirmed The new routing is in the CR, but kcp couldn't confirm every pod applied it. Check the Gateway (operator acceptance, pods) before anything else. A re-run reads only the CR, sees the topics routed to the destination and reports nothing to do. Ctrl+C or lost connection The fence stays. Re-run execute.

Resume with a manifest that resolves to the same topics. kcp recognizes the fence it added by its exact shape: a rules.fencing entry with only topics (the batch's topic set) and blocked: true. If the topic set changes between runs, kcp treats the earlier fence as yours and leaves it on the route, so those topics stay blocked after the switch. Finish the interrupted batch first. If it has already happened, remove the leftover blocked entry from the route's rules.fencing by hand. For how each run reconciles and resumes, see Execution model.

docs.title: Run the next batch
docs.text:
After a batch completes, the route is still dynamic with the same two bound domains. Its rules now have one routing condition for the batch and an empty fencing list:

rules:
  routing:
    coordination:
      group: source-kafka-cluster
    default: source-kafka-cluster
    conditions:
      - topics: ["t1.order", "t1.inventory"]
        streamingDomain: confluent-cloud
  fencing: []

For the next batch, write a new manifest with the next topics and run it the same way. kcp prepends one condition per batch, so the list grows, up to a size cap on the whole rules block. If the cap is hit, kcp refuses with a message to migrate a smaller batch.

Validate each batch before starting the next: confirm its clients are producing and consuming against Confluent Cloud, and its mirrors are STOPPED (kcp migration cutover lag-check shows each mirror's status). Re-running kcp migration cutover execute --dry-run on the batch's manifest reports nothing to do.

docs.title: After the last batch
docs.text:
When every topic on the cluster link has been promoted, the route is still dynamic and consumer groups are still coordinated by the source. Run a conversion to make the route static and move group coordination to the destination. KIP-848 consumers only come onto the migrated route after it is static.

The source cluster stays on the route until the conversion. Decommission it after the conversion, when you are sure nothing connects to it directly.
