docs.title: Convert a Dynamic Gateway Route to Static
docs.text:
A conversion closes out a topic-based migration on Confluent Gateway. It replaces the dynamic route with a static route bound to the destination, and copies each consumer group's committed offsets to the destination so group coordination moves too.

When every topic you're migrating has moved to Confluent Cloud, the route is still dynamic: it binds both clusters, and consumer group coordination is still pinned to the source. After the conversion, clients reconnect to the same Gateway address, and the source is no longer on the route.

This guide walks through the prerequisites, the migration manifest, and a conversion run. For how conversions fit with the other migration types, see Gateway migrations.

Early Access

Dynamic routing is an Early Access feature of Confluent Private Cloud Gateway 1.4, intended for evaluation and non-production testing. Its configuration schema might change before general availability. A conversion closes a dynamic migration, so it needs a dynamic route.

docs.title: Prerequisites and limitations
docs.text:
Gateway

  • The Gateway runs on Kubernetes and is managed by Confluent for Kubernetes (CFK). kcp reads and patches the Gateway custom resource (CR), so a Gateway started any other way can't be converted.
  • The route to convert is dynamic: it binds exactly two streaming domains, the source and the destination, and sets rules.routing.coordination.group to the source.
  • The destination is one of the two bound domains, its binding carries a bootstrapServerId, and the route already carries security.cluster.<domain> authentication for it. This is already true if you ran a dynamic migration on the route.
  • The route carries no fence kcp didn't write, and no route-level fence. A fence left by an unfinished dynamic migration batch is the usual cause of a refusal. See Refusals.
  • Gateway 1.4.0 and later, and CFK 3.4.0 and later. See Version requirements.

Cluster link

  • The cluster link that the dynamic migration used still exists, and every mirror topic on it is promoted (STOPPED). The link is the conversion's scope: its mirror topics are the topics in scope, and the consumer groups that commit only on them are in scope too. A conversion selects no topics.
  • Each link topic has the same name on both clusters, so the link has no cluster.link.prefix, and the same partition count on both clusters.
  • Every link topic is routed to the destination by the dynamic route. Finish any unfinished batch first.
  • Keep the link until the conversion is done. Don't delete it after the last batch: its mirror topics are kcp's only record of which topics were migrated, and kcp works out the in-scope consumer groups from those topics. Without the link, kcp can't read the scope and the run fails with an error reading the link's mirror topics.
  • Keep the source topics too. Deleting a source topic purges its consumer groups' committed offsets, so the conversion has nothing to copy for it, and the source can no longer accept offset commits on it.

  • Consumer offset sync is off for the link, as it was during the dynamic migration. kcp refuses otherwise. The conversion copies the offsets itself, so you don't turn sync back on.

  • The route has one cluster link: every batch of the dynamic migration used it. One link maps to one route and one conversion. The manifest names a single link and the conversion's scope is that link, so topics migrated over any other link are outside it, and a consumer group that commits on one of them refuses the conversion. kcp doesn't check that the route's batches all used the same link, so this is yours to keep to.

Consumer groups

  • A source consumer group whose committed offsets are all on link topics is in scope, and its offsets are copied to the destination.
  • A group with a committed offset on a topic that isn't on the link refuses the conversion. After the switch that topic isn't reachable through the route, or the group belongs to a client outside it.
  • kcp checks every group on the source cluster, not only the route's. That includes groups that commit on Kafka Streams changelog and repartition topics or Kafka Connect internal topics, so put those topics on the link or retire the group first.
  • An in-scope group with live members on the destination refuses the conversion, and so does a destination share group with the same name as an in-scope group. Detecting a share group clash needs a destination that reports group types, which Kafka 3.8 and later do. A group that exists on the destination with no members gets a warning, because its offsets are overwritten.

Clients

  • Every producer and consumer connects through the Gateway. The conversion's fence only blocks traffic that goes through it. kcp checks for consumers that commit to the source directly, but not for producers.
  • Producers use acks=1 or acks=all, and a delivery.timeout.ms longer than the pause (see What clients see). With acks=0 they never see the fence's errors and their records are dropped.
  • KIP-848 consumers (group.protocol=consumer) can't use a dynamic route. They work on the static route after the conversion finishes.

Limitations

  • The whole route pauses, not a batch. Every topic on the route is blocked from the fence to the switch.
  • The point of no return is the switch. A failure before it removes the fence and leaves the route as it was. After the switch, kcp can't roll the route back to dynamic.
  • Ctrl+C leaves the fence in place. Re-run execute to continue.
  • A conversion needs at least one promoted topic on the link. It closes a topic-based migration rather than replacing one.
  • Only committed offsets and their metadata are copied. Group configuration, share group state, and transactional state aren't.
  • The unrouted-commit check sees only what changes between its two snapshots, including a removed group, an admin reset, or expired offsets. A commit after the second snapshot isn't seen, and that consumer re-reads from the copied offset.

Access

  • Credentials for the source, the destination Apache Kafka® listener, and the cluster link REST API, each as a credentials file.
  • The source and destination credentials must be able to list every consumer group and describe every topic. A credential that sees only part of a cluster would hide a group or topic from kcp's checks. The destination credential must also be able to write consumer group offsets (READ on the groups and the topics). On an MSK IAM source, that means kafka-cluster:DescribeGroup and kafka-cluster:DescribeTopic on every group and topic resource.
  • A Kubernetes identity that can read and patch the Gateway CR, read its Deployment, and list its pods. With hot reload on, it also needs get on pods/proxy and a cluster-scoped get on the Gateway custom resource definition (CRD). See Permissions for the full Role and the Kafka grants.

docs.title: How a conversion works
docs.text:
kcp keeps no state between runs. Each run reconciles the manifest against the live Gateway, both clusters, and the cluster link, and continues from wherever they already are. For a conversion the stages are:

  1. Fence. kcp adds a fence that blocks every topic on the route (topicPatterns: ['.*'], blocked: true) at the head of the route's rules.fencing, and waits for every Gateway pod to apply it. Clients get errors they can retry, and they buffer in the meantime.
  2. Verify. On data read after the fence, kcp re-runs the checks that decide whether the route can be converted, confirms its own fence is still on the route, and re-runs the credential, cluster link, and consumer group checks. It then takes two snapshots of every source group's committed offsets, detectUnroutedCommitsDuration apart. If any offset changed, a client is committing to the source directly, and kcp aborts and unfences the route.
  3. Sync offsets. kcp writes each in-scope group's committed offsets, with their metadata, to the destination. It refuses the whole sync if an offset is past its destination partition's high-water mark.
  4. Switch. kcp replaces the dynamic route with a static route bound to the destination, with no rules (so no fence). security and the rest of the route are kept. This is the point of no return.

A conversion has no promote stage: every topic was promoted in the dynamic migration, and a conversion refuses to start until they are.

As in a migration, kcp works out how the Gateway applies a new configuration, in place (hot reload) or by rolling its pods, and waits for every pod to confirm each change. rolloutTimeout and hotReloadTimeout bound those waits.

A failure before the switch removes the fence and leaves the route as it was. Offsets already written to the destination have no effect until the switch.

docs.title: What clients see
docs.text:
• A pause. Every topic on the route is blocked from the fence to the switch: about detectUnroutedCommitsDuration (30 seconds by default) plus two Gateway reloads. Producers retry. Consumers fetch nothing and can't commit.
  • A rejoin, and possibly a re-read. After the switch, the consumers' group coordinator is on the destination. Each consumer's first commit or heartbeat there fails, because the destination doesn't know its member, so it rejoins its group and resumes from the copied offset. It might read again what it fetched between the switch and that first failed commit or heartbeat, and what it consumed just before the fence but couldn't commit. For a consumer that commits after every batch, that is up to one poll (max.poll.records). For one that auto-commits, it is up to the backlog the fence built. This is expected at-least-once behavior. Nothing is skipped.

docs.title: 1. Finish the dynamic migration
docs.text:
Before you write the manifest:

  • Every batch has completed, and every mirror topic on the link is STOPPED.
  • No fence is left on the route's rules.fencing from an interrupted batch or other reason.
  • Every application that uses the route is ready for the pause, and its producers meet the client requirements.

docs.title: 2. Write the migration manifest
docs.text:
The manifest declares the conversion with spec.dynamicToStaticConversion. Everything outside that section is the same as in the dynamic migration, so you can start from the last batch's manifest. Every credentials field is a path to a credentials file, and the manifest holds no secrets. Paths resolve relative to the working directory you run kcp from.

apiVersion: kcp.confluent.io/v1alpha1
kind: GatewayMigration

metadata:
  name: msk-prod-to-cc-convert

spec:
  source:
    type: msk # msk | apache-kafka
    bootstrapServers:
      - b-1.msk-prod.abc123.c2.kafka.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:9096
    # Must be able to list every consumer group and describe every topic.
    credentials: /etc/kcp/source-creds.yaml

  target:
    type: confluent-cloud # confluent-cloud | confluent-platform
    clusterId: lkc-abc123
    kafka:
      bootstrapServers:
        - pkc-xxxxx.us-east-1.aws.confluent.cloud:9092
      restEndpoint: https://pkc-xxxxx.us-east-1.aws.confluent.cloud:443
      # Must also write consumer group offsets: the conversion copies the
      # source's committed offsets here.
      clusterCredentials: /etc/kcp/dest-kafka-creds.yaml

  clusterLink:
    name: msk-to-cc # the link the dynamic migration used
    linkCredentials: /etc/kcp/link-creds.yaml

  gateway:
    namespace: confluent
    cr-name: gateway-initial

  dynamicToStaticConversion:
    route:
      name: migration-route # the dynamic route the migration used
      targetStreamingDomain: confluent-cloud # one of the two domains the route binds
    # No topicGroup: a conversion covers every mirror topic on the link.
    policies:
      detectUnroutedCommitsDuration: 30s # 0s uses the built-in 30s; never skipped; minimum 10s
      offsetSyncConcurrency: 0 # workers reading and writing offsets; 0 uses the built-in 8
      rolloutTimeout: 10m
      hotReloadTimeout: 90s

Notes on the choices above:

  • A conversion manifest has no topicGroup, consumerOffsetSync block, lagThreshold, or promoteBatchSize. A conversion's scope is the cluster link, and it has no promote stage.
  • detectUnroutedCommitsDuration is off by default, like its producer counterpart in a migration. When set, it is also how long every topic on the route is blocked, so raising it lengthens the pause.
  • rolloutTimeout defaults to no deadline, so a rollout that never converges waits indefinitely with traffic already fenced. Set one.
  • offsetSyncConcurrency matters only when you have many consumer groups. Each worker holds its own broker connection.

The complete annotated manifest is gateway-route-conversion.yaml. Every field, validation rule, and policy default is in the migration manifest reference.

docs.title: 3. Dry run
docs.text:
kcp migration cutover execute --migration-yaml migration.yaml --dry-run

A dry run validates the manifest and credentials, then reads the live Gateway CR, both clusters, and the cluster link, and prints the plan: the route checks, the link's topics, and the consumer groups in scope. It changes nothing and exits non-zero if the plan is refused. Run it until it passes.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
A run is refused, with nothing changed, when any of the following is true:

  • The route isn't dynamic, doesn't bind exactly two domains, doesn't bind the target, or doesn't pin coordination.group to the source.
  • Consumer offset sync is still enabled on the cluster link.
  • A link topic is still ACTIVE, is still being promoted, is routed to the source, is named differently on the destination, or has a different partition count on the destination, or no topic on the link is promoted at all.
  • A consumer group commits on a topic that isn't on the link, or an in-scope group has members on the destination.
  • A credential can't list every group, describe every topic, or write offsets.
  • The route has a fence kcp didn't write, or a route-level fence.

The conversion reference lists the fix for each. Two need care:

  • A fence kcp didn't write. Find out what it is for before you remove it. If it belongs to an unfinished dynamic migration batch, finish that batch instead: removing its fence would send producers back to a source topic the link no longer mirrors. Otherwise remove it, because the conversion drops it.
  • A group commits on a topic that isn't on the link. Migrate the topic, delete the group's stale offsets on it or the group itself, or stop the application that owns it.

kcp also warns, without refusing, about source topics that aren't on the link and that no group commits on: after the switch, the route sends their traffic to the destination.

docs.title: Run the conversion
docs.text:
Schedule a window. Every client on the route is paused from the fence until the switch.

kcp migration cutover execute --migration-yaml migration.yaml

You can override any policy for a single run with its flag, for example --detect-unrouted-commits-duration 60s. See the command reference.

When it finishes, kcp prints Route conversion completed: <metadata.name>. Re-running a finished conversion reconciles to nothing to do.

docs.title: If a run stops
docs.text:
Where it stopped What happened What to do Before the fence (refused plan) Nothing was changed. Fix the cause and re-run. After the fence, before the switch (for example unrouted commits) kcp removes the fence and leaves the route as it was. Offsets already written to the destination have no effect. Fix the cause (for example send the client through the Gateway) and re-run. Switch failed, static route never reached the Gateway CR The fence stays. Fix the cause and re-run execute to finish. Switch failed, route reached the CR but wasn't confirmed The new route is in the CR, but kcp couldn't confirm every pod applied it. Check the Gateway (operator acceptance, pods). Don't re-run: it would report nothing to do. Ctrl+C or lost connection The fence stays. Re-run execute with the same manifest.

kcp doesn't clean up when it is stopped (Ctrl+C, SIGTERM, or a crash), so a killed run leaves the fence up and the route keeps blocking every topic until you re-run the same manifest. If a re-run is refused while kcp's fence is on the route, kcp warns you. Fix the refusal and re-run, or remove kcp's entry from rules.fencing by hand.

docs.title: After the conversion
docs.text:
After a conversion, the route is static and bound to the destination, with no rules:

routes:
  - name: migration-route
    endpoint: bootstrap.gw.example.local:9595
    brokerIdentificationStrategy:
      type: host
      pattern: "broker$(nodeId).gw.example.local"
    mode: static
    # Bound to the destination only. streamingDomains and rules are gone.
    streamingDomain:
      name: confluent-cloud
      bootstrapServerId: SASL_PLAIN
    security:
      client:
        authentication:
          type: none
        tls:
          secretRef: client-tls
      cluster:
        # Kept by the conversion. Unused now that the route doesn't bind the source.
        source-kafka-cluster:
          auth: passthrough
        confluent-cloud:
          auth: swap
          secretStore: file-store
          authentication:
            type: plain
            jaasConfigPassThrough:
              secretRef: plain-jaas

kcp leaves the source's security.cluster entry on the route and the source's entry in the CR's spec.streamingDomains. Neither carries traffic. Remove them when you decommission the source, and keep the top-level domain while any other route still uses it.

  • Confirm clients rejoined their groups on Confluent Cloud, are producing and consuming, and resumed from the copied offsets. To compare a group on both clusters, see Migrate consumer groups.
  • Re-running kcp migration cutover execute --dry-run reports nothing to do.
  • Consumer group coordination is now on the destination. KIP-848 consumers (group.protocol=consumer) can connect through the route. Switching a consumer to the new protocol is a client change that kcp doesn't make.
  • Transactional producers, like KIP-848 consumers, can use the route now that it is static.
  • The source cluster is no longer on the route. Decommission it on your own schedule, after you are sure nothing connects to it directly.

After the conversion finishes, kcp no longer needs the cluster link. Delete it when you no longer need it.

After the switch, a conversion only moves forward. kcp doesn't move clients back to the source after that point, so validate with --dry-run before the window.

docs.title: Idempotency and Resumability of Gateway Migrations
docs.text:
You can re-run kcp migration cutover execute after any failure, interruption, or completed migration. This page explains, for each workflow, what a re-run does and doesn't do.

For what to do at each failure point, see the "If a run stops" table in the guide for your workflow: static, dynamic, or conversion.

docs.title: How a run works
docs.text:
kcp keeps no state between runs: no state file, lock, run ID, or marker on a cluster. metadata.name in the manifest labels the log lines and is never written anywhere. What survives a run is only what it left on external systems, listed in What a run leaves behind.

Every run does the same two things:

  1. Reconcile, once. kcp reads the manifest, the live Gateway custom resource (CR), both clusters, and the cluster link, and classifies each topic (or, for a conversion, the route and the link's scope). A refusal is all-or-nothing: if any check fails, nothing is changed. If nothing is left to do, the run stops here and exits zero.
  2. Walk the steps. kcp walks the full list of steps for the workflow from the first. The reconcile plan decides each step: a step either has nothing to do, or applies its change again. kcp doesn't re-check the live state for each step along the way.

Re-applying a completed step is safe, but some steps cost time again:

  • Fence. A resume re-patches the fence even if it is already on the route. The value is identical, but the patch carries a fresh spec.configId, so it can cost another hot reload or pod roll before kcp moves on. An identical dynamic fence entry is replaced, never duplicated.
  • Offset sync pause (static). kcp waits the consumerOffsetSyncDrainDuration again, then sets the configuration to false again.
  • Unrouted-producer window. The full detectUnroutedProducersDuration window runs again, with clients still blocked. A conversion likewise repeats its detectUnroutedCommitsDuration window.
  • Lag wait. Polls again from the start.

docs.title: What a run leaves behind
docs.text: Where What Workflows Gateway CR route The fence (see below). Dynamic also adds a routing condition for the batch. All Gateway CR spec.configId A random kcp-<hex> value, set by every patch when the Gateway supports it. Never cleaned up. Also set once by the hot-reload check at the start of the fence step, so a run that fails after the lag wait has already changed it, with no effect on traffic. All, with hot reload Cluster link consumer.offset.sync.enable, and each mirror's status. Promotion is irreversible. Configuration: static. Mirrors: static and dynamic. Destination Committed consumer group offsets. Conversion kcp.log Diagnostic only. kcp never reads it back. All

docs.title: How kcp recognizes its own fence
docs.text:
kcp doesn't tag its fence. It recognizes it by exact shape, and anything else is treated as yours:

  • Static: a route-level fence of exactly scope: ALL with the defaulted error code, BROKER_NOT_AVAILABLE. An operator's plain scope: ALL fence reads back identically, so kcp can't tell it from its own and removes it. Any other non-NONE fence is refused.
  • Dynamic: a rules.fencing entry with only topics and blocked: true, where topics is exactly this batch's resolved set. Any other entry, such as one with a trafficType key or a different topic set, is treated as an operator's. The fence, the switch, and a rollback all leave it untouched.
  • Conversion: a rules.fencing entry over every topic. Any other rules.fencing entry is refused as a foreign fence.

Two kcp migrations that produce the same shape can't be told apart.

docs.title: Static
docs.text: Step On a re-run Check lag Skipped when no topic needs promoting. A run with only promoted-but-unswitched topics skips it but still fences, verifies, and switches. Otherwise polls again, with no timeout. Fence Re-patched. Skipped only if the plan has nothing to fence. Pause offset sync Waits the drain duration, then sets the configuration again. Skipped unless pause is set and the plan has a fence to apply. Verify the fence The full window runs again, and covers promoted-but-unswitched topics too, because writes to a promoted topic's source are never copied. It fails if a source offset rises or offsets can't be read. Skipped if the duration is 0s. Promote Mirrors already STOPPED aren't promoted again. Mirrors in PENDING_STOPPED are awaited, not promoted again. A promote error is retried up to three times per topic, then the run fails. Switch Skipped if the route is already bound to the destination. Restore offset sync Runs only when owed: pause is set and either this run migrated topics or the link's live setting differs from baseline.

docs.title: Dynamic
docs.text: The same steps without the offset sync pause and restore. A dynamic migration doesn't touch offset sync, and refuses a link that has it enabled.

docs.title: Conversion
docs.text:
Step On a re-run Fence Re-patched. Verify the fence Never skipped. kcp re-gathers every fact, re-runs the route, credential, and link checks, and takes two offset snapshots a window apart. Sync offsets Commits every group's offsets again. Commits are idempotent, so a partial earlier attempt, or a rollback and redo, repeats them harmlessly. Switch Replaces the route. Skipped if the route is already static on the destination.

A conversion has no lag or promote step.

docs.title: Ctrl+C and crashes
docs.text:
Ctrl+C, SIGTERM (a canceled CI job, a pod eviction), and a crash all end the process where it is, and kcp doesn't roll back or clean up. Whatever is on the cluster stays, which typically means:

  • The fence is on the route.
  • For a static migration with pause: true, offset sync is still paused.
  • Mirrors might be part-way through promotion.

The next run finds the fence by its shape, continues from the first step, and repeats the work in How a run works. If a resumed run fails before reaching its own fence step, it removes the earlier fence, unless rollback is no longer allowed.

docs.title: Interrupted during promote
docs.text: The cluster link finishes any promotion it has already accepted, whether or not kcp is running. A re-run finds those mirrors in PENDING_STOPPED, waits for them to reach STOPPED and doesn't promote them again. With promoteBatchSize set, a run that stops between batches resumes by waiting for the batch in flight and then promoting the rest.

docs.title: Where rollback stops
docs.text:
Until the point of no return, a failure removes the fence and restores offset sync, and traffic returns to the source.

Workflow Rolled back on failure during Point of no return Static The fence, and the offset sync pause The start of promote, even if nothing has been promoted yet Dynamic The fence, including the unrouted-producer check The start of promote Conversion The fence, the verify step, and the offset sync The switch

Rollback is also off from the start of a run that finds a topic already promoted or promoting, because sending those clients back would split them from the destination. In that case even an early failure, such as a lag error, keeps the fence.

A fence that was written but not confirmed. If kcp patched the fence but couldn't confirm that every pod applied it, kcp rolls it back even if it appears not to have landed, because it could still take effect after kcp exits. Only a run where rollback isn't allowed keeps the fence. This rollback also restores offset sync, and it can cost another hot reload or pod roll.

When the rollback itself has a problem.

  • The offset sync restore after a rollback is best effort. If it fails, kcp prints the command to run by hand.
  • If removing the fence fails on a static or dynamic abort, kcp logs the error and returns the original failure, so the fence might still be on the route. Check the Gateway CR.
  • A conversion, and the unconfirmed-fence rollback on any workflow, report the rollback failure alongside the original one.

When a producer writes to the source after rollback stops. If the unrouted-producer check fails after the point of no return, the fence stays. Stop the producer or route it through the Gateway, then re-run.

docs.title: Re-run a finished migration
docs.text:
A finished static or dynamic migration prints Migration completed: <name> with nothing to do: no topic in it still needs migrating, and exits zero. A finished conversion prints Route conversion completed: <name> with nothing to do: the route is already static on its target domain. In both cases only the reconcile reads happen: no Gateway patch, no capability probe, no promote.

Two cases are not "nothing to do":

  • Static with pause: true. If the link's consumer.offset.sync.enable no longer equals consumerOffsetSync.baseline, kcp runs the restore step and sets it back. If you turned offset sync off on purpose after the cutover, a re-run turns it back on. kcp takes baseline from the manifest because the link doesn't record the value it had before, so update baseline to the state you want, or skip the re-run.
  • A switch that was applied but not confirmed. Reconcile reads the Gateway CR, not the pods. If the switch reached the CR but kcp couldn't confirm every pod applied it, the next run sees the topics routed to the destination and reports nothing to do. For a conversion kcp tells you not to re-run. For static and dynamic migrations it doesn't, so check the Gateway's acceptance and pods before you re-run.

docs.title: Change the manifest between runs
docs.text:
kcp reads policies, credentials, and flags fresh on every run. An environment variable named like a policy flag overrides the manifest without telling you.

Change Effect Dynamic: the resolved topic set changes The earlier fence is no longer recognized as kcp's. It stays on the route after the switch, and a rollback doesn't lift it. Remove the leftover blocked entry by hand. Dynamic: a source topic is deleted mid-way The run is refused: <topic> not found on the source. Static: the topic selection changes The fence is recognized by shape, so it isn't orphaned. The route still flips as a whole. A topic dropped from the selection while still ACTIVE is cut over without being promoted. Static: pause is set to false on a resume No restore is owed and no rollback restore runs. A link that an interrupted run paused stays paused. targetStreamingDomain changes Reconcile evaluates against the live route. Mid-fence, the run proceeds with the new target if it is declared and staged. After completion it is refused. clusterLink.name changes Mirrors are read from the new link, so topics not on it fail the run as not on the cluster link. Dynamic: batches overlap Tolerated. Completed topics are unchanged, and only the rest is fenced.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
kcp doesn't coordinate concurrent runs: it uses no lock, lease, or resourceVersion check. The guard is on each Gateway patch. It tests the route's index and the field being overwritten against the value kcp read moments earlier, so a concurrent edit between kcp's read and its patch makes the patch fail.

Some cases fall outside that guard:

  • Drift since reconcile. The fence, switch, and rollback are computed at reconcile time. An edit made to the route between reconcile and the patch, for example during a long lag wait, can be overwritten.
  • Concurrent batches on one dynamic route. Each writes the whole rules block, so they can overwrite each other. Run one batch at a time.
  • Two runs of the same migration. Each patch stamps a new configId, so one run's per-pod wait can time out because the other superseded it.

kcp can't tell when a GitOps controller reverts its fence, so consider pausing syncing on the Gateway CR for the duration of the cutover.

docs.title: What --dry-run guarantees
docs.text:
--dry-run runs reconcile and stops there, and exits non-zero if the plan is refused. It makes no Gateway write, link configuration write, promote, or capability probe.

Reads it performs: the Gateway CR, the Gateway's Deployment and pods (and, with hot reload on, each pod's /config), topic lists and cluster IDs on both clusters, the link's state, mirrors, and configurations, and for a static migration the staged Secrets. A conversion also lists groups, describes topics, reads offsets and partition counts, and sends one write probe: an offset commit for a group and topic that don't exist, to test the destination credential. It creates nothing.

Because it stops there, a passing --dry-run doesn't exercise the Kubernetes patch permissions, the cluster-scoped hot-reload grant, or the link write permission. See Permissions for what to grant ahead of a real run.

docs.title: Gateway Migration Limitations
docs.text:
This page covers the boundaries of kcp migration cutover itself, so you can plan around them.

Limits that come from Confluent Gateway, such as dynamic routing being Early Access, no transactions or share groups on a dynamic route, no KIP-848 consumers, and the host broker identification strategy, are in the Gateway migrations overview. Limits that apply to one workflow only are in the guide for that workflow.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
• kcp doesn't create the cluster link or its mirror topics. Set them up before the run, for example with kcp migration resources create.
  • Mirrors must be healthy. kcp understands ACTIVE, STOPPED, and PENDING_STOPPED. A mirror in any other state, such as FAILED or PAUSED, stops the run with <topic> mirror is in a failed/transitional state.
  • A manifest covers one route, and for static and dynamic migrations one topic group per run.

docs.title: Connections and authentication
docs.text:
• kcp connects directly from the machine it runs on to the source and destination brokers, the link's REST endpoint, and the Kubernetes API, so each needs to be reachable from there.
  • kcp's own Apache Kafka® connections support iam (MSK source only), sasl_scram (SHA-256 or SHA-512, stated explicitly), sasl_plain, mtls, unauthenticated_tls, and unauthenticated_plaintext. OAUTHBEARER and Kerberos aren't available for kcp's own connections, even where the Gateway supports them.
  • Sources are msk or apache-kafka. confluent-platform isn't accepted as a source, and MSK Serverless isn't supported. See Source compatibility.
  • The Kubernetes context is the kubeconfig's current one. The manifest has no field to pick another, so select it in the kubeconfig before the run.
  • Credentials are file paths, not inline blocks or environment variables, and paths resolve against the working directory.

docs.title: Cluster link
docs.text:
• A static migration doesn't check offset sync. Dynamic migrations and conversions refuse a link with consumer.offset.sync.enable on. A static migration checks neither that setting nor consumer.offset.group.filters, so confirm the filters include the groups you want to move.
  • Cluster ID checks can be skipped. kcp compares the link's source_cluster_id with the source cluster's ID, and spec.target.clusterId with the destination's. If an ID is empty, for example on a Confluent Platform version that doesn't report source_cluster_id, that comparison is skipped.
  • kcp's lag can differ slightly from lag-check. kcp computes lag from partition offsets on both clusters, while kcp migration cutover lag-check shows the lag the link reports.
  • Link REST requests have no timeout and aren't retried, so a transient failure such as a 429 or 5xx ends the step. Before promote, kcp rolls the fence back. During promote, the fence stays and a re-run continues.

docs.title: Topic selection
docs.text:
• Patterns use RE2 syntax and match the whole topic name. The Gateway uses Java-style patterns, so constructs such as lookahead, backreferences, and possessive quantifiers aren't accepted, either in the manifest or in the routing conditions of the live Gateway custom resource (CR). The manifest has no exclude list, so write patterns that name what you want to include.
  • topicPatterns: ['.*'] selects every topic the broker doesn't flag as internal, and each one needs to be a mirror on the link or the run is refused. If your cluster holds topics that aren't mirrored, such as monitoring topics, prefer patterns or literal names that cover your application topics.

docs.title: Waits and timeouts
docs.text: Wait Bound Lag before the fence None. The run stops after three consecutive offset read failures. Zero lag after the fence, and mirrors reaching STOPPED None. kcp waits for exactly zero, whatever lagThreshold is, with the fence in place. Operator acceptance and Gateway rollout rolloutTimeout. Default: no deadline. Per-pod configuration wait (hot reload) hotReloadTimeout. Default: 90 seconds.

docs.title: How kcp verifies a Gateway change
docs.text:
kcp decides how to confirm a change from spec.hotReload.enabled on the live Gateway CR. If the field is absent, kcp treats hot reload as off.

  • Hot reload on. Before the fence, kcp patches spec.configId alone on the live CR and waits for every pod to report it on GET /config (port 9180 unless policies.gatewayConfigPort says otherwise). A Gateway on a trial license doesn't run its configuration watcher, so its pods never apply the change and kcp stops before the fence. For the grants this needs, see Permissions.
  • Hot reload off. kcp waits up to 10 seconds for the Gateway's Deployment generation to change. If it doesn't, kcp takes that to mean no pod restart was needed. kcp doesn't read what each pod applied, so if the operator updates the Deployment later than that, or applies a change in place another way, check the Gateway's state before you move on.

--dry-run doesn't run these checks.

docs.title: What to confirm yourself
docs.text:
kcp works from the Gateway CR, the clusters, and the link. A few things sit outside what it can observe, so confirm them before a cutover:

  • Producers that bypass the Gateway. kcp checks for these only when you set detectUnroutedProducersDuration, which is off by default. The check compares two source offset snapshots a window apart, so it sees only producers active during the window, on the topics in this run's selection.
  • Consumers that bypass the Gateway. A conversion checks for these. For static and dynamic migrations, make sure every consumer in a group connects through the Gateway, so the group isn't split across two coordinators.
  • Route topics that aren't selected or mirrored. On a static route these move to the destination along with the rest of the route, without a warning.
  • The streaming domains' endpoints. kcp doesn't compare a streaming domain's endpoint with the clusters in the manifest, so confirm that the source and destination domains point where you expect.
  • The fallback route. kcp reads routing.default as the fallback domain, so declare the fallback there rather than as unmatchedTopics.
  • Gateway Secrets and security.cluster. What kcp checks differs by workflow (see Gateway secrets). It never reads Secret contents, external stores such as Vault or AWS Secrets Manager, or the TLS settings for the host strategy. A problem there surfaces when the Gateway or CFK rejects the fence or the switch, after the lag wait.
  • Client settings. acks, transactions, share groups, and the group protocol aren't visible to kcp. See the guide for your workflow for what each needs.

docs.title: Dynamic migration
docs.text:
• Each batch adds a routing condition to rules, and kcp doesn't compact them. A fence or switch that would make the rules block larger than 512 KiB is refused with rules block within size limit, so narrow the selector or migrate a smaller batch.
  • A fence you wrote over the same topics is left untouched. kcp warns about shadowing for conditions that name a topic exactly, but not for pattern conditions.
  • kcp treats the other bound domain as the source. Beyond the cluster ID check, kcp doesn't verify that it is the cluster the link mirrors.

docs.title: Gateway Migrations Overview
docs.text:
kcp migration cutover execute cuts clients over from your source Apache Kafka® cluster to Confluent Cloud without asking them to change their configuration. It does this through the Confluent Gateway: your applications connect to the Gateway, and a route on the Gateway decides which cluster their traffic reaches.

Kubernetes and CFK only

kcp orchestrates Gateway migrations only when the Gateway runs on Kubernetes and is managed by Confluent for Kubernetes (CFK). kcp reads and updates the Gateway custom resource (CR) through the Kubernetes API, so a Gateway started directly from its Docker image, or by any other means, can't be migrated with kcp migration cutover execute. The Gateway images are published on Docker Hub as cpc-gateway, confluent-gateway, and confluent-gateway-for-cloud.

A cutover changes where the route points, and the clients follow. A route has a mode, and the mode decides which kind of migration you can run:

Route mode Migration type Cuts over Consumer group coordination static All-at-once (AAO) Every topic on the route, together Moves with the cutover dynamic Topic-based (TBM) Selected topics, in batches Stays on the source until the route is converted

A third workflow, the dynamic-to-static conversion, closes out a topic-based migration by changing the route's mode after every topic has moved.

This page introduces the three. Each gets a detailed guide of its own. For the field-by-field manifest syntax, see the migration manifest reference.

How kcp picks the workflow

You declare the workflow in the migration manifest by including exactly one of spec.staticMigration, spec.dynamicMigration, or spec.dynamicToStaticConversion. kcp reads the live Gateway resource on every run and refuses to continue if the route's mode doesn't match what you declared. A static migration can only run on a static route, and a topic-based migration only on a dynamic one.

docs.title: How every cutover works
docs.text:
All three workflows follow the same shape. kcp keeps no state between runs: every run reconciles the manifest against the live Gateway, both clusters, and the cluster link, and continues from wherever the live state already is. If a run is interrupted, re-run the same command.

Resuming moves forward, and rolling back is only possible early on. Until the point of no return, a failure removes the fence and traffic returns to the source. After it, kcp never rolls back, and a failure leaves the fence in place until a re-run completes the migration. The point of no return is the start of the promote step for static and dynamic migrations, and the switch for a conversion.

  1. Fence. The Gateway starts rejecting client traffic for the topics being moved, so nothing is written to the source while the destination catches up. Clients see errors they can retry, and they buffer in the meantime.
  2. Promote. kcp promotes the mirror topics on the cluster link after they have caught up with the source.
  3. Switch. kcp updates the route to point at the destination and removes the fence. Clients reconnect to the same Gateway address and land on Confluent Cloud.

Run kcp migration cutover execute --dry-run at any point to see the plan and any refusals without changing anything.

docs.title: Version requirements
docs.text:
• Gateway 1.4.0 and later. kcp v0.11.0 and later support Gateway 1.4.0 and later. For a Gateway on 1.3.x, upgrade the Gateway first or use kcp v0.10.x.
  • CFK 3.4.0 and later. Dynamic routing is Early Access in Gateway 1.4 and CFK 3.4. See the CFK release notes.
  • Hot reload. If the Gateway CR sets spec.hotReload.enabled: true, the operator's Gateway custom resource definition (CRD) must also declare spec.configId. kcp checks this before the fence. If the field is missing, kcp refuses and names the ways to proceed, one of which is setting spec.hotReload.enabled: false for the duration of the migration. For how kcp confirms each pod applied a change, see How kcp verifies a Gateway change.

docs.title: Static routes (all-at-once)
docs.text:
A static route binds all of its traffic to one streaming domain. A static migration fences the route as a whole, promotes every selected mirror topic, and flips the route to the destination in a single cutover.

Use it when

  • The workload can tolerate one short pause, and you would rather have one cutover than many.
  • Topics are tightly coupled (for example transactional workloads) and must move together.
  • You want consumer group coordination to move with the cutover, with the cluster link syncing committed offsets across.

Things to know

  • The whole route pauses, not only the topics you selected. Topic selection only decides which mirrors are promoted and lag-checked.
  • The route must already carry authentication for the destination, staged ahead of time, so the cutover itself needs no secret or auth change.
  • Consumer offset sync should be on for the cluster link. kcp does not check this for a static route.
  • The point of no return is the start of the promote step. After it starts, kcp never rolls back: a failure leaves the fence in place and the next run continues forward.

docs.title: Dynamic routes (topic-based)
docs.text:
A dynamic route binds two streaming domains, the source and the destination, and sends each topic to one or the other according to routing rules. A topic-based migration moves a batch of topics at a time: it fences only those topics, promotes their mirrors at zero lag, and updates the routing so those topics now go to Confluent Cloud. Everything else keeps flowing to the source.

The Gateway side of this, including the routing rules and fencing, is documented in Migrate Topics Incrementally with Topic-Based Routing and Fencing. Read it before planning a topic-based migration.

Early Access

Dynamic routing is an Early Access feature of Confluent Private Cloud Gateway 1.4, intended for evaluation and non-production testing. Its configuration schema might change before general availability. Fencing itself is generally available.

Use it when

  • You want to migrate incrementally, application by application or domain by domain, with time to validate between batches.
  • A single whole-route pause is not acceptable.
  • You want a smaller blast radius for each step.

Things to know

  • Each batch is its own manifest, and batches must contain disjoint topics.
  • Resume an interrupted batch with a manifest that resolves to the same topics. If the set changes between runs (a topic added or removed, or a pattern that now matches a new topic), kcp treats the earlier fence as one you authored and leaves it on the route, so those topics stay blocked after the migration completes.
  • The route must bind exactly two streaming domains, with consumer group coordination pinned to the source.
  • The cluster link's consumer offset sync must be off, and kcp refuses to run otherwise. Consumer groups stay coordinated by the source cluster while the route is dynamic.
  • Transactions and share groups are not supported on a dynamic route. Migrate transactional workloads with a static migration.
  • Consumers must use the classic group protocol. KIP-848 consumers (group.protocol=consumer) can't use a dynamic route at all, for the whole life of a topic-based migration. They work on a static route, so if you have them, use a static migration.
  • Only the host broker identification strategy is supported, which requires TLS configuration on the route.
  • SCRAM isn't supported for client or cluster authentication on a dynamic route. Use PLAIN or OAUTHBEARER.
  • Topic auto-creation isn't supported, and some consumer group admin APIs are unavailable, so tools such as kafka-consumer-groups don't work against a dynamic route.
  • Fencing pauses produce or consume traffic only. Producers with acks=0 can't see the errors, so their records for fenced topics are silently dropped. Use acks=1 or acks=all.
  • A fence can't stop clients connected to the source directly. The check for producers that bypass the Gateway (detectUnroutedProducersDuration) is off by default in kcp.
  • All members of a consumer group must connect through the route, or the group splits across two coordinators.
  • A topic-based migration leaves the route dynamic. Finish the job with a conversion.
  • Dynamic routes need Gateway 1.4.0 and later, and CFK 3.4.0 and later. See Version requirements.

docs.title: Dynamic-to-static conversion
docs.text:
After every topic on the cluster link has been migrated, the route is still dynamic, and consumer groups are still coordinated by the source cluster. A conversion changes the route's mode from dynamic to static, bound to the destination, and copies each consumer group's committed offsets across so that group coordination moves too. Topics don't change. The route's mode does.

Use it when

  • A topic-based migration has finished and you are ready to retire the source for these clients.
  • Your clients include KIP-848 consumers, which can't connect through a dynamic route and so only come onto the migrated route after it is static.
  • You want the route back in its simplest form.

Things to know

  • A conversion selects no topics. The cluster link is its scope: every mirror topic on it must already be promoted, with the same name and partition count on both clusters.
  • It briefly fences every topic on the route. kcp watches committed offsets on the source for a window (30 seconds by default) to catch consumers that bypass the Gateway, and fails if it sees any.
  • Consumers rejoin their group on the destination after the switch and resume from the copied offset. They might re-read a small amount of data. Nothing is skipped.
  • The switch is the point of no return. A failure before it removes the fence and leaves the route as it was.
  • Conversion is refused for a cluster link that uses cluster.link.prefix, and for consumer groups that commit offsets on topics outside the link.

docs.title: Choose a workflow
docs.text:
If you need… Choose One cutover and one pause for everything on the route Static migration To move topics in stages and validate in between Dynamic migration, then conversion Topics that must move together to preserve transactions Static (dynamic routes don't support transactions) KIP-848 consumers Static migration (dynamic routes don't support them) The smallest pause per step Dynamic migration

kcp changes a route's mode in one direction only: dynamic to static, with a conversion. It doesn't make a static route dynamic. To run a topic-based migration on a route that is static today, change the route yourself before the first batch: bind both domains, pin coordination.group to the source, and set routing.default to the source. Two things to check first:

  • A dynamic route needs the host broker identification strategy and client TLS. If the static route uses something else, the change affects how clients connect, so plan it as a separate change ahead of the migration.
  • KIP-848 consumers and transactional producers can't use a dynamic route. If the route has any, use a static migration instead.

docs.title: Permissions for Gateway Migrations
docs.text:
kcp migration cutover execute talks to five things: the Kubernetes API, the source Apache Kafka® cluster, the destination Kafka cluster, the cluster link's REST API, and, indirectly, the cluster link itself. Each one needs its own identity, and this page lists what each identity needs, which workflow needs it, and what you see when it is missing.

For the credentials file formats, see Credentials. For where each connection is used, see Connections.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Identity Where you set it What kcp does with it Kubernetes spec.gateway.kubeconfig (or the pod's service account) Reads and patches the Gateway custom resource (CR), reads its Deployment and pods. Source Kafka spec.source.credentials Read-only: topic metadata and offsets. Conversion also lists groups and reads their offsets. Destination Kafka spec.target.kafka.clusterCredentials Read-only for static and dynamic. Conversion also writes consumer group offsets. Cluster link REST spec.clusterLink.linkCredentials Reads link state, mirrors, and configurations. Promotes mirrors. A static migration with pause writes a configuration. The link's own credential Set when the link was created Not used, read, or checked by cutover. It decides whether the link itself can read the source.

Every write kcp makes is to the Gateway CR, the cluster link, or, for a conversion, the destination's consumer group offsets. kcp never writes to the source cluster.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text: kcp builds its client from spec.gateway.kubeconfig, expanding a leading ~/. With no kubeconfig set, it uses the pod's service account when it runs inside a cluster, and ~/.kube/config otherwise. A kubeconfig is used at its current context. The manifest has no field to pick another one. The namespace comes only from spec.gateway.namespace.

docs.title: Role
docs.text:
Grant this in the Gateway's namespace:

rules:
  - apiGroups: ["platform.confluent.io"]
    resources: ["gateways"]
    verbs: ["get", "patch"]
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["deployments"]
    verbs: ["get", "list"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods"]
    verbs: ["list"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods/proxy"]
    verbs: ["get"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["secrets"]
    verbs: ["get"]
Resource and verb Needed when gateways: get Always, including --dry-run. gateways: patch Any real run. kcp applies the fence, the switch, and any rollback as JSON Patches. deployments: get Any real run: kcp reads the Gateway's Deployment generation before each patch and while waiting for the rollout. Also --dry-run when hot reload is off, to check that the rollout has finished. deployments: list Only as a fallback, when no Deployment is named like the Gateway CR. kcp then finds the one owned by the CR. pods: list Always, including --dry-run. kcp lists the Gateway's pods to check that they serve the Gateway CR. pods/proxy: get The Gateway has spec.hotReload.enabled: true, including --dry-run. kcp reads each pod's /config through the API server to check the pods' revision, and again after each change to confirm the new one. secrets: get Optional, static migrations only. See below.

Every run, including --dry-run, first checks that the Gateway's pods serve the Gateway CR as it stands. With hot reload off, kcp checks that the operator has caught up with the CR, that the Deployment has finished rolling out, and that no replaced pod is still terminating. With hot reload on, it checks that the operator has caught up and that every Ready pod reports the CR's spec.configId. If any of these fails, kcp refuses the run and shows what it observed. Re-run once the rollout has completed.

The secrets grant is optional. A static migration checks that every Secret referenced by the staged security.cluster.<destination> block exists, by name, without reading its contents. If the identity can't read Secrets, kcp skips the check and warns. A confirmed missing Secret still refuses the run. The Confluent operator, not kcp, reads the Secrets at runtime.

docs.title: Cluster-scoped grant for hot reload
docs.text:
When the live Gateway CR has spec.hotReload.enabled: true, kcp also reads the Gateway custom resource definition (CRD) to confirm the operator declares spec.configId:

apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["apiextensions.k8s.io"]
    resources: ["customresourcedefinitions"]
    resourceNames: ["gateways.platform.confluent.io"]
    verbs: ["get"]

kcp uses spec.configId to confirm that each pod applied a hot reload, so without this grant it can't check that the field is declared, and it refuses before fencing. The refusal names two ways out: grant the permission, or set spec.hotReload.enabled: false in the live CR for the duration of the migration.

docs.title: When a Kubernetes grant is missing
docs.text:
Missing What you see gateways get failed to produce the reconcile plan: loading gateway config: reading gateway CR ..., with the API server's 403 text. Before anything changes. gateways patch failed to apply fenced gateway CR: ... at the fence step. A rollback patch needs the same grant. deployments get failed to get gateway deployment: .... With hot reload off, the pod check fails with it before anything changes. Otherwise it appears while waiting for a rollout, and after the fence kcp rolls the fence back where it can. pods list checking gateway "<name>" pods: failed to list gateway pods: ..., with the API server's 403 text. Before anything changes. CRD get (hot reload) A refusal before the fence, naming the grant (see above). pods/proxy get (hot reload) A refusal from the pod check, before anything changes, naming the pod that did not answer GET /config. kcp can't tell a missing grant from a network failure, so check the grant first. If the grant is lost after that check, you see only timed out after 90s waiting for the gateway to apply the configId on every pod.

For the Gateway and Confluent for Kubernetes (CFK) versions that hot reload needs, see Version requirements.

docs.title: Source Kafka cluster
docs.text:
kcp only reads from the source, with whichever of iam (MSK only), sasl_scram, sasl_plain, mtls, unauthenticated_tls, or unauthenticated_plaintext you put in the credentials file. With iam, kcp signs with the AWS credential chain on the machine it runs on, and that principal needs the MSK kafka-cluster:* actions for the calls below.

What kcp reads Used by Kafka access control list (ACL) Topic metadata and cluster ID All workflows DESCRIBE on topics Partition offsets (lag, unrouted-producer check) All workflows DESCRIBE on topics Every consumer group, with its committed offsets Conversion DESCRIBE on all groups and all topics

A credential that lacks DESCRIBE on a topic doesn't fail loudly. It sees fewer topics, and kcp reports <topic> not found on the source. If you see that for a topic you know exists, check the ACL before anything else.

docs.title: Destination Kafka cluster
docs.text:
The destination credential is separate from the link REST credential, and kcp never derives one from the other. It can be any of the types above except iam. On Confluent Cloud this is a cluster API key and secret, used as the SASL/PLAIN username and password. A sasl_plain credential with neither a CA certificate nor tls: true is forced to TLS.

What kcp does Used by Kafka ACL Topic metadata and cluster ID All workflows DESCRIBE on topics Partition offsets (lag, promotion at zero lag) All workflows DESCRIBE on topics Lists every consumer group and describes every topic Conversion DESCRIBE on all groups and all topics Commits each group's offsets Conversion READ on all groups and all topics

On Confluent Cloud, grant these to the API key's service account with ACLs or the equivalent role bindings.

docs.title: Cluster link
docs.text: kcp doesn't create the link. It must exist, with its mirror topics, before the run.

docs.title: REST credential
docs.text:
linkCredentials is a cluster-scoped credential, sent to restEndpoint as api_key plus api_secret, basic, bearer, or mtls.

Call Used by Describe the link All workflows, lag-check List mirror topics All workflows, lag-check List link configurations All workflows Promote mirror topics Static, dynamic Set consumer.offset.sync.enable Static, and only with consumerOffsetSync.pause: true

Dynamic migrations and conversions only read the link. A static migration with pause: true writes one configuration, twice: it pauses offset sync after the fence and restores it after the switch. That write happens after the fence, so a credential that can read but not write fails the run mid-cutover. kcp then rolls the fence back, and the rollback restore needs the same write permission.

Status What you see 401 or 403 describing the link authentication failed (status N) followed by a prompt to verify the target REST credentials 404 cluster link "<name>" not found on cluster <id> 401 or 403 on a configuration write authentication failed (status N) while SET "consumer.offset.sync.enable" ... 403 on list mirrors, list configurations, or promote The raw status and body, for example unexpected status code 403. These aren't translated.

docs.title: The link's own credential
docs.text:
The link reads the source with the credential it was created with. Cutover never reads, sets, or verifies this credential, and can't see it. If it is short, the symptom is mirrors that don't catch up or offsets that don't sync, not a kcp permission error.

The link's credential needs READ, DESCRIBE, and DESCRIBE_CONFIGS on the topics you mirror, and with offset sync on, READ and DESCRIBE on the consumer groups it syncs. An MSK link uses SCRAM, because a cluster link can't use IAM credentials. On MSK, these are therefore Kafka ACLs.

See Migrate consumer groups for how this plays out in a static migration.

docs.title: Gateway secrets
docs.text:
kcp doesn't hold the destination's credentials during a cutover. The route must already carry security.cluster.<destination> authentication, with its secret store and Secrets present, before the run (see Stage the destination on the Gateway). The checks differ by workflow:

  • Static: the staged block must exist and its referenced Secrets must exist (subject to the optional secrets grant above).
  • Dynamic: kcp doesn't check security.cluster or its Secrets. A problem shows up when the operator rejects the patch.
  • Conversion: the security.cluster.<destination> block must exist. kcp doesn't check Secrets.

If the operator rejects the applied CR, for example for a missing secretRef, kcp reports gateway "<name>" was rejected by the Confluent operator with a kubectl command to read the conditions, after a 30 second settle window.

docs.title: Conversion credential checks
docs.text:
A conversion probes its Kafka credentials during reconcile, so --dry-run finds these before any change. It re-runs them after the fence. The probes use fixed sentinel group and topic names, so they test wildcard-level access: an identity with ACLs scoped to a prefix fails them even if it could cover the groups you have. A failing probe skips the later link checks, so fixing one credential can reveal the next.

Refusal Grant it asks for Source or destination credential can't list every group DESCRIBE on all consumer groups (an ACL on *, or with MSK IAM, the DescribeGroup action on every group) Source or destination credential can't describe every topic DESCRIBE on all topics (an ACL on *, or with MSK IAM, the DescribeTopic action on every topic) Destination credential can't write consumer group offsets READ on all consumer groups and all topics (ACLs on *)

The offset-write probe commits an offset for a group and topic that don't exist and reads the authorization error. The probe doesn't create a group. If a broker accepts it anyway, kcp tells you which group to delete.

docs.title: Migrate With a Static Gateway Route
docs.text:
A static migration moves all topics on the route to Confluent Cloud in a single cutover, with no client configuration changes.

Your applications already connect to the Confluent Gateway. A static route binds all of its traffic to one cluster, so cutting over means pausing the route, promoting the mirror topics on the cluster link, and repointing the route at the destination. Clients reconnect to the same Gateway address and land on Confluent Cloud.

This guide walks through the prerequisites, the migration manifest, and a cutover run. For how static migrations compare with topic-based ones, see Gateway migrations.

docs.title: Prerequisites and limitations
docs.text:
Gateway

  • The Gateway runs on Kubernetes and is managed by Confluent for Kubernetes (CFK). kcp reads and patches the Gateway custom resource (CR), so a Gateway started any other way can't be migrated.
  • The route to migrate is static: it has a single streamingDomain bound to the source cluster.
  • The destination is already declared on the Gateway CR as a streaming domain with exactly one bootstrap server ID, and the route already carries security.cluster.<destination> authentication for it, with its secret store and Secrets present. The cutover is a pure streamingDomain flip, so no secret or auth change happens during it. See Stage the destination on the Gateway.
  • The route carries no fence of its own. kcp refuses a route with a fence it didn't add.
  • Gateway 1.4.0 and later, and CFK 3.4.0 and later. See Version requirements.

Cluster link

  • A cluster link from the source to the destination already exists, and every topic you select is a mirror topic on it. kcp migration cutover never creates either. To set them up, use kcp migration resources create.
  • Consumer offset sync should be on for the link, so committed offsets reach the destination. kcp doesn't check this. A link created with kcp migration resources create has offset sync on for every group by default. See spec.clusterLink.
  • Mirror lag must be at or below lagThreshold (default 0, fully caught up) before kcp fences the route.

Clients

  • Every producer and consumer connects through the Gateway. The fence only blocks traffic that goes through it, so a producer writing to the source directly keeps writing.
  • Producers use acks=1 or acks=all. Fenced clients get an error they can retry, and they buffer in the meantime. With acks=0, producers never see the error, and their records are dropped.
  • Consumer groups move with the cutover. KIP-848 consumers (group.protocol=consumer) and transactional workloads are supported on a static route.

Limitations

  • The whole route pauses, not only the topics you select. Topic selection decides which mirrors are promoted and lag-checked.
  • A manifest migrates one route and one topic group per run.
  • The point of no return is the start of promote. After it, kcp never rolls back. A failure leaves the fence up until you re-run and the migration completes.
  • Ctrl+C leaves the fence in place. Re-run execute to continue.
  • A static migration has no per-topic staging. If you need to move topics in stages, use a topic-based migration.
  • Create the cluster link without cluster.link.prefix. kcp expects each mirror topic to have the same name on both clusters.
  • Cutover doesn't migrate schemas. Move them before the cutover, for example with kcp iac schemas generate.

Access

  • Credentials for the source, the destination Apache Kafka® listener, and the cluster link REST API, each as a credentials file.
  • A Kubernetes identity that can read and patch the Gateway CR, read its Deployment, and list its pods. With hot reload on, it also needs get on pods/proxy and a cluster-scoped get on the Gateway custom resource definition (CRD). For the full Role, see Permissions.

docs.title: How the cutover works
docs.text:
kcp keeps no state between runs. Each run reconciles the manifest against the live Gateway, both clusters, and the cluster link, and continues from wherever they already are. On a static route the stages are:

  1. Check lag. Every selected mirror topic must be within lagThreshold.
  2. Fence. kcp adds a route-level fence (scope: ALL, errorCode: BROKER_NOT_AVAILABLE) and waits for every Gateway pod to apply it. Clients get errors they can retry, and they buffer in the meantime.
  3. Pause offset sync (optional). If consumerOffsetSync.pause is set, kcp waits consumerOffsetSyncDrainDuration, then disables the link's offset sync. Pausing keeps the link from writing offsets to the destination during promote. For when to use it, see Migrate consumer groups.
  4. Verify the fence. If detectUnroutedProducersDuration is set, kcp reads the source's partition offsets, waits that duration, and reads them again. If any offset advanced, a producer is still writing to the source directly, and kcp aborts and unfences the route instead of promoting.
  5. Promote. kcp promotes the mirror topics, in batches of promoteBatchSize, and waits for each to stop mirroring. This is the point of no return.
  6. Switch. kcp flips the route's streamingDomain to the destination and removes the fence.
  7. Restore offset sync (if paused). kcp sets the link's consumer offset sync back to the state you declared in consumerOffsetSync.baseline, the state it was in before the migration.

A failure before promote removes the fence and restores offset sync, so traffic returns to the source.

docs.title: 1. Stage the destination on the Gateway
docs.text:
The route starts bound to the source. The destination is declared next to it, with swap authentication staged on the route, so the switch needs no further change. This is the part of the CR that matters for a static migration. The rest is your normal Gateway configuration.

apiVersion: platform.confluent.io/v1beta1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: gateway-initial
  namespace: confluent
spec:
  secretStores:
    - name: file-store
      # ...
  streamingDomains:
    - name: source-kafka-cluster
      type: kafka
      kafkaCluster:
        bootstrapServers:
          - id: UNAUTHED
            endpoint: PLAINTEXT://source-kafka.confluent.svc.cluster.local:9071
    # Declared ahead of time so the cutover is only a field flip.
    - name: destination-kafka-cluster
      type: kafka
      kafkaCluster:
        bootstrapServers:
          - id: SASL_PLAIN
            endpoint: SASL_SSL://destination-kafka.confluent.svc.cluster.local:9071
  routes:
    - name: migration-route
      endpoint: gateway-initial.confluent.svc.cluster.local:9595
      # Singular streamingDomain makes this a static route.
      streamingDomain:
        name: source-kafka-cluster
        bootstrapServerId: UNAUTHED
      security:
        client:
          authentication:
            type: none
        cluster:
          source-kafka-cluster:
            auth: passthrough
          # Staged ahead of time: swap auth for the destination.
          destination-kafka-cluster:
            auth: swap
            secretStore: file-store
            authentication:
              type: plain
              jaasConfigPassThrough:
                secretRef: plain-jaas

kcp checks this staging on every run, before anything is fenced, and --dry-run reports it.

To build the route yourself, see the CFK documentation for routes, authentication swapping, and secret stores.

docs.title: 2. Write the migration manifest
docs.text:
The manifest declares the migration with spec.staticMigration. Every credentials field is a path to a credentials file, and the manifest holds no secrets. Paths resolve relative to the working directory you run kcp from.

apiVersion: kcp.confluent.io/v1alpha1
kind: GatewayMigration

metadata:
  name: msk-prod-to-cc-batch-1

spec:
  source:
    type: msk # msk | apache-kafka
    bootstrapServers:
      - b-1.msk-prod.abc123.c2.kafka.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:9096
    credentials: /etc/kcp/source-creds.yaml

  target:
    type: confluent-cloud # confluent-cloud | confluent-platform
    clusterId: lkc-abc123
    kafka:
      bootstrapServers:
        - pkc-xxxxx.us-east-1.aws.confluent.cloud:9092
      restEndpoint: https://pkc-xxxxx.us-east-1.aws.confluent.cloud:443
      clusterCredentials: /etc/kcp/dest-kafka-creds.yaml

  clusterLink:
    name: msk-to-cc # must already exist on the destination
    linkCredentials: /etc/kcp/link-creds.yaml

  gateway:
    namespace: confluent
    cr-name: gateway-initial

  staticMigration:
    route:
      name: migration-route # the static route in the Gateway CR
      targetStreamingDomain: confluent-cloud # declared in the CR, with staged auth
    topicGroup:
      - topics: ["t1.order", "t1.inventory", "t2.order"]
        # topicPatterns: ['orders\..*'] # RE2, matched against the full topic name. ['.*'] selects every source topic, so every one must be mirrored on the link.
    consumerOffsetSync:
      pause: true
      baseline: enabled # what to restore after the switch
    policies:
      lagThreshold: 0
      promoteBatchSize: 100
      rolloutTimeout: 10m
      detectUnroutedProducersDuration: 30s # 0s skips the check; minimum 10s
      consumerOffsetSyncDrainDuration: 15s

Notes on the choices above:

  • topicGroup takes literal topics, anchored topicPatterns, or both (the union), and has no default. To migrate everything, write topicPatterns: ['.*'].
  • detectUnroutedProducersDuration is off by default. If you can't rule out producers bypassing the Gateway, turn it on.
  • rolloutTimeout defaults to no deadline, so a rollout that never converges waits indefinitely with traffic already fenced. Set one.
  • consumerOffsetSync.baseline is the offset sync state to restore after the switch. Set it to what the link has now, normally enabled.

The complete annotated manifest is gateway-static-migration.yaml. Every field, validation rule, and policy default is in the migration manifest reference.

docs.title: 3. Dry run
docs.text:
kcp migration cutover execute --migration-yaml migration.yaml --dry-run

A dry run validates the manifest and credentials, then reads the live Gateway CR, both clusters, and the cluster link, and prints the plan: each precondition and a verdict per topic. It changes nothing and exits non-zero if the plan is refused. Run it until it passes.

docs.title: 4. Watch the lag
docs.text:
kcp migration cutover lag-check --migration-yaml migration.yaml

lag-check shows replication lag for every mirror topic on the link, whatever the topic selection. It only needs the link REST credentials, so you can run it long before the cutover.

docs.title: Run the cutover
docs.text:
Schedule a window. Clients are paused from the fence until the switch.

kcp migration cutover execute --migration-yaml migration.yaml

You can override any policy for a single run with its flag, for example --detect-unrouted-producers-duration 60s. See the command reference.

When it finishes, kcp prints Migration completed: <metadata.name>. Re-running a completed migration reconciles to nothing to do.

docs.title: If a run stops
docs.text:
Where it stopped What happened What to do Before the fence (refused plan, lag above threshold) Nothing was changed. Fix the cause and re-run. After the fence, before promote kcp removes the fence and restores offset sync. Traffic returns to the source. Fix the cause (for example an unrouted producer) and re-run. During or after promote The fence stays. Rolling back would split promoted topics from their clients. Fix the cause and re-run execute. It rolls forward. Switch reached the CR but wasn't confirmed The new route is in the CR, but kcp couldn't confirm every pod applied it. Check the Gateway (operator acceptance, pods) before anything else. A re-run reads only the CR, sees the route bound to the destination and reports nothing to do. Ctrl+C or lost connection The fence stays. Re-run execute.

Don't change the manifest's topic selection between an interrupted run and its resume unless you mean to.

docs.title: After the cutover
docs.text:
• Confirm clients reconnected and are producing and consuming against Confluent Cloud.
  • The source cluster is no longer on the route. Decommission it on your own schedule, after you are sure nothing connects to it directly.
  • If you paused offset sync, confirm the link is back at your consumerOffsetSync.baseline.
  • kcp migration cutover lag-check shows every selected mirror STOPPED, and re-running kcp migration cutover execute --dry-run reports nothing to do.
  • To compare a consumer group on both clusters, see Migrate consumer groups.

After promote starts, a migration only moves forward. kcp doesn't move clients back to the source after that point, so validate with --dry-run and lag-check before the window.

docs.title: Discover Transactional Workloads
docs.text:
This guide walks you through finding the transactional workloads on your source cluster before you plan a migration, so you know which topics must move to Confluent Cloud together.

Most topics in an Apache Kafka® cluster are independent of one another. You can move clickstream to Confluent Cloud today and user-profiles next month, and neither notices. Transactional workloads are the exception. When a producer writes to several topics inside one Kafka transaction, those writes commit or abort together, and downstream consumers reading with isolation.level=read_committed rely on that all-or-nothing behavior. If you cut those topics over on different days, a single transaction ends up split across two clusters, and the guarantee the application was built on is gone.

To find them, you run a small standalone utility, txn-discovery, against your source cluster, let it watch for a while, and get back a list of transaction groups: sets of topics that must move together. You can migrate everything it doesn't put in a group one topic at a time.

Proof of concept

txn-discovery is an exploratory utility that lives in the kcp repository under utils/transaction-discovery. It is not part of the kcp binary, and no kcp command reads its output. Treat the results as input to your own migration planning, and review them before acting on them.

docs.title: Prerequisites and considerations
docs.text:
Cluster support

  • Supported: self-managed Apache Kafka, Confluent Platform, and AWS MSK Provisioned. These expose the __transaction_state internal topic for reading.
  • Not supported: Confluent Cloud and MSK Serverless. They don't expose __transaction_state, so the utility stops at its first check with an error naming the topic.

Access

  • A principal that can read internal topics. For the exact access control lists (ACLs), see Grant permissions.
  • Network access from the machine running the utility to the source brokers.

Build tooling

  • Go 1.25 and later to build the utility. The result is a single static binary with no runtime dependencies, so you can build once and copy it to whichever host can reach the cluster.

Time

  • The utility reports what it observed, so it needs to run long enough to see your transactional workloads. Plan for anywhere from a few minutes (to try it out) up to a week (to catch infrequent jobs). See Choose an observation window.
